utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kalco.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I hope you had a good rest.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, you mentioned Mr. Marko Lujic yesterday, and a document was produced seemingly showing that he was a member of the brigade sometime in the early days of the conflict. Could the usher or the registrar please get the document Z1009.1. When you get the document, you will have a look at it. But as we are waiting, perhaps -- Nihad Rebihic, he was an intelligence officer in your staff, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you know that he wrote several reports to the 3rd Corps about the security, of course, but also about individuals considered responsible for crimes in the Lasva Valley; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at item 1 on this document? "Marko Lujic, son of Marko," and here will you look, please, to the end of the document. Is that "Rebihic"; will you agree with that? This is a document which has already been tendered and admitted. Now, if you look at this description, Marko Lujic's activity described here does not seem to indicate in any way at all that he was a member of the brigade. Have you ever seen this report?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You know about it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you then agree with what I'm putting to you, that this description, written by your men, has nothing to do with the person who would be a gunner in the field?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, this act is dated the 2nd of June, 1993, and Marko Lujic was a gunner, an artilleryman, at the time of the first conflict in Ahmici, when we prevented the HVO forces to pass on to Novi Travnik. Yesterday, I said that we recorded, on a tape, the conversation between Marko Lujic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, you know that Marko Lujic has a son whose name is Mario?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Wasn't perhaps that conversation between him and that son?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only with Marko Lujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, perhaps I was not clear enough. Was it perhaps a conversation -- or at least we put it to you that it was a conversation between Marko Lujic and his son Mario.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday, you told us quite a lot about that car bomb on the 18th of April in Stari Vitez which went off.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But there are certain perplexities about this. Some say 18th, some 19th, but we shall agree it was the 18th.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 18th at half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And not to go back to various papers anymore, in your statement to the investigators on the 15th and 16th of July, 1995, that is, at the time when your memory was much fresher, you told them, and I shall read it out: "On the 19th of April, 1993, on the third day of the attack at 1300 hours in the British Battalion compound in Bila, a meeting was held between the BiH and the HVO. Sefkija Djidic was present, and Mario Cerkez and Brkovic. Blaskic and General Merdan were high military officers." And the last sentence: "In the course of the meeting, at 1700 hours, from the direction of the Catholic Church, a cistern filled with four tonnes of explosives was driven by a driver tied up in the truck." First, I suppose that it was a confusion when you say the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is an error. Perhaps it was a translation mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And at any rate, it describes it here, because it says "three days after the attack," so we agree with that. It also transpires from this that at this time, Mario Cerkez and your commander, Djidic, was either at the BritBat or on his way back.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with this, except that at the time when the explosion took place --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, Mr. Kalco, may I ask you to try to go through my questions, and then my learned friend for the Prosecution may ask you additional questions.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but may I simply add something about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Kovacic, what is it that you want to ask this witness about the incident? We'll get on more quickly if we deal with it in an orderly way. What is it that you want to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Djidic and Cerkez were in BritBat and on the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the witness wanted to add something to his answer, in relation to that. Yes, Mr. Kalco.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. At a meeting at the British compound, first came Sefkija in Stari Vitez, when the Warrior opened, and which were both Mario and Sefkija Djidic. I told Sefkija Djidic about the car bomb, and at that moment Mr. Mario laughed cynically. That is all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was about to ask you whether they had arrived in a Warrior. And as for this cynical smile, could you see his face well?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that is how you saw it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, yesterday you told us a great deal about a certain Miroslav Bralo; Cicko, rather. You were asked a number of questions about him. Pursuant to the JNA concept -- and you say that you took it over, and that you also supposed that the HVO had done the same -- who was responsible to initiate disciplinary proceedings and ordering disciplinary detention for military? Is it the direct superior of that particular military?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander, the commander of a unit turns the individual over to the relevant prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I shall ask you to look at a document. Indeed, we can all see documents. Mr. Kalco, the first document that you have, you have the English version, and then below it the Croat original. It says "85" on the Croatian version. Are we looking at the same document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could it be placed on the ELMO, please. So this is the document of the military police in Vitez of the 3rd February 1993. And could we get a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be numbered D62/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The one from 3rd February.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kalco, will you please look at the heading and the signature. This document seems to show that the detention of Miroslav Bralo, and disciplinary detention at that, rather, military detention, immediately after the act had been committed, was ordered by Pasko Ljubicic. In view of what you just told us, I believe that this indicates the hierarchy, that is, who is vested with the responsibility.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Tell me, then, this. The reasons indicated here for ordering the detention said that Bralo planted an explosive in Esad Salkic's house. You mentioned him already, didn't you? So will you agree with me, this is a document of the 4th Battalion of the military police, and that the person is Pasko Ljubicic, whom you also mentioned in your conversations?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, but first answer me just this. Is this the Pasko Ljubicic that you mentioned yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is. Yes. His signature. But for Pasko Ljubicic to issue an order on the detention, he had to get the order from the unit commander that such and such an individual was being turned over, that is, Miroslav Bralo was being turned over to the military police on such and such date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But who is Pasko Ljubicic's superior?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that Mario Cerkez was Cicko Bralo's commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what if Pasko Ljubicic was commander; in that case who would be issuing such a warrant?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The superior commander, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Will you then look at the next document dated 11th February. You also have the English version first and then the Croatian version. This is a decision of the relevant District Military Court in Travnik ordering detention during investigation. So this is court detention for Bralo while the investigation is underway. Have you ever seen a document of this kind?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you, perhaps, know the judge who signed there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, very well. He is my friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Zeljko Percinlic, did he hold this same position as then, that is a judge in the District Military Court?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And will you now look at the third document, the 26th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Number for the second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for the second document is D63/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the third document of the 26th of March, the judge extends the detention during -- pending the completion of investigation, the same judge. Have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the judge is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, it is not the same judge. It is already the trial judge, because an indictment had been issued, so it is after the investigation.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And do you know this judge?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maric, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And he was a judge at the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And yet another document to do with Miroslav Bralo. Carry Spork testified about 2483.2, and tab 23 are some documents related to Miroslav Bralo. And there is a document marked Z1465.4. Maybe, to save some time, Your Honour, could I just show the witness my document, because that is coming from the binder, and I don't know how that is numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was on this document, a report on the wounding, signed by the commander of the battalion that, first, somebody wrote the period of service of Miroslav Bralo with the brigade, and then it was amended by hand, and that amendment was initialled. It transpires from this document that Bralo was with the brigade between the 7th of August 1993 until the 19th of September 1993. Have you ever seen this document or heard about it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Neither heard nor seen. All I know is that this is an invalid document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has not seen it before. This is pointless, showing it to him. Return it to counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask for the signature, does he know the person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look. Why don't you get this evidence confirmed by your own witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is Prosecution evidence. I just want to ask the witness whether he knew anything about that, because there was some indication that he might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How is it going to help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a long story, but there are a couple of documents relating to Bralo. They are very conflicting amongst them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can put it to the witness to see if he recognises the signature, "yes" or "no". Yes, put it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'll just ask him the name. There is no need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought you wanted the witness to identify the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Not really the signature, Your Honour, but the name of this commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, will you please tell us, if you can read the name, Vlatko Matosevic, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. But above that is Mario's signature as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about Matosevic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was he a soldier in that brigade, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you're saying that Cerkez initialled that document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move on to another subject. Yesterday, you spoke about an incident when Ivan Sucic, your colleague and a member of Cerkez' team, was detained by the military police of the army. You said that actually he turned out to be drunk, and you said that obviously he got drunk because of the holiday. It was during Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, we were shown Document Z462. Could we please have a look at it? The witness saw it yesterday, actually. [In English] No, no, it's Z462. Yesterday, it was given. Sorry, it is my lapse. 642. Good. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the English go onto the ELMO. Let the witness have the -- if it's possible, to have the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, I would like to draw your attention to the beginning of section 4. This is Cerkez' letter. You saw it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in section 4, in paragraph 4, it says that Slavko Mlakic, a judge in the military court in Travnik, and Ivan Sucic were going back from the Easter mass. Do you agree that it was during Easter?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know. I can't remember. I don't know. I can only say that they were not detained by the military police or the authorities of the BH army in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar please show the witness Document D54/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, could you please have a look at this document, and please pay attention to the signatories. The contents of this document show that this was one of the meetings where attempts were made to continue with some kind of cooperation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Another thing, by the way, now that we've got this document in front of us. In the introduction, where those who are present were mentioned, your name is there too, you were present, and also there was the representative of the staff of Vitez, Marijan Skopljak. Did he take part in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let us proceed. Yesterday, you spoke to us quite a bit about the Vitezovi. Yesterday, you saw a document from the Prosecutor, Z661. Could you please have a look at it again? Two things, please. First of all, in the middle of the last paragraph, the last paragraph on the first page, and it starts with the word "DEMAND" in capital letters, Kraljevic spoke about extremes on both sides, as far as I understood it; that is to say, people who were acting to the detriment of both peoples. Do you agree that both parties had their own extremists?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. When one party acts in extremist fashion, then the other one tries to respond. However, it was the Croat side that was always the first to start, and they had more extremists. This document relates to Kraljevic before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please look at the stamp next to his signature. It's quite legible, and it says: "PPN Vitezovi, The Defence Department." Can you conclude, on that basis, who this unit belongs to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me continue. Just an additional question related to these extremists that you confirmed, in a way. Mr. Kalco, can one say that during 1992 in your municipality, there were actually frequent incidents, regardless of who caused them, and then the other side would return, and then there would be peace, and then this would happen again, and then the politicians would act; is that a correct assessment for 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us move on to another subject. You mentioned your visit to the cinema yesterday, that is to say, your visit to the detainees and the meeting. It wasn't said specifically. Perhaps it should be put into a context. These meetings or, rather, this visit on the 30th of April, wasn't it the result of the ceasefire agreement that was signed at a higher level and then here at the Petkovic-Halilovic level?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was signed at a higher level. I just know that Petkovic and Sefer Halilovic signed an agreement on ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Obviously, this visit was aimed at the implementation of this agreement, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Usher, I have no need for that document anymore. You can remove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cerkez and his command had some offices in this same cinema building near the hotel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the first floor?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you visited him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You saw him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, a certain number of Bosniak Muslims were detained in the school in Dubravica. Did you visit that school?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Which did you visit? You visited the cinema, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the cinema and the public accounting service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, did you notice which services or which units were securing, guarding these buildings?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you not see that they belonged to the military police? Didn't they have such insignia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very little. Mainly it was the HVO from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know who held the school in Dubravica, who held that detention centre?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew -- I found out later that it was the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about Kaonik, which is outside our municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next subject that I wanted to ask you about, and we would just like to clarify what you said in this connection, the offensive of the HVO against Stari Vitez on the 18th of July, 1993. That is the one that happened during the summer. There is no doubt that Darko Kraljevic was in charge; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic was in charge of this action which started from the direction of Princip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the direction of the garages, Novi Vitez. Nakic was in charge, and I don't know who was on the other side from the church, from the Rajic/Bilic houses. I don't know who was there. I just know there was Nakic and Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I imagine that Dario Kordic is a slip of the tongue?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. It was Kraljevic. I really apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As a soldier, I believe that you agree that this action was coordinated from several directions. As you said, it had to have a commander, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it wouldn't have been carried out otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In your last interview at the OTP on the 5th of March, you said that Darko Kraljevic on his own was in charge of this action?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the translation was not good. He was in charge of that action that took part -- that took place from the direction of Princip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there is another Nakic, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is this other Nakic who was in the military police. Not Franjo Nakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So Nakic from the military police?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then you said, in connection with the action concerning the collection of the dead bodies, the soldiers' dead bodies, and you said that Boro left 15 bodies and said, "These were not ours. They were not from Vitez."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first we did not know how many soldiers there were. We ascertained this only later. Boro Jozic said, "These are not soldiers of the Viteska Brigade or, rather, from Vitez." Later, as I said, we realised that they were from Osijek, Daruvar, because we found their documents, their military IDs and their family photographs, et cetera. We handed that over to the authorities in charge in Zenica. I don't know what happened to this afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, okay. Let's leave that. Mr. Kalco, tell me about these IDs of these soldiers. Did you see this personally?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps notice on these IDs and these documents, at least on some of them, that they were issued by the HOS?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the Croatian army. Not the HVO. The Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I am not sure whether we have understood each other. I am asking you whether the HOS had issued some of these documents.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The HSP party?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about the time when these documents were issued? Do you, perhaps, remember some of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. And as for the birthplaces of these persons, were these persons from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Perhaps their parents were. All of them were born there, in Osijek, Daruvar, et cetera, the places I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Apropos, since we've already mentioned Boro Jozic, you know that he was killed in front of his house in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Boro Jozic does not have a house in Vitez. He has an apartment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I meant when I said house, in front of the apartment building where he lived. And you didn't know this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You knew him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you never heard that he was killed in front of his building that faces Old Vitez, in front of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it, but the question is who killed him, the BiH army or the HVO, because there is the possibility of either side having killed him. No one is ever going to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you think that the HVO did it? Do you think that this was a bullet that went astray or what?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that at that time the army did not fire at the apartment buildings, the Kolonija, towards that part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But there was a similar incident when Marko Prskalo, a negotiator from Blaskic's staff, was hit in front of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, what has this got to do with the examination-in-chief or this trial? It seems to me that we are going off on a chase, on a totally different topic. And we really must concentrate on the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will not go further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move onto another subject, Mr. Kalco. The question relates to the military model of subordination or, as you military men like to say, the resubordination, the attachment of units. You said that according to the JNA concept a unit that came to a certain territory would have to be subordinated to the highest unit in that territory.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. And that is the model that the army and the HVO abided by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you agree with that, unless the order specified otherwise?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like you to have a look at some documents, two or three of them, but the first one by way of an example. Could the Registrar give the -- give Document 91/1 to the witness, please. Mr. Kalco, I would like to use this document by way of an example.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had that particular one that had -- let me tell you one thing. I can't read half of this. Do you have the Croatian text?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have the Croatian text, but it's a poor photocopy. But I'm sure you can see one thing there. Please look at this signature, the bottom of the other page. Is that Blaskic? Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And it also says who copies were sent to. Just look at this, to all the formation in the operative zone of Central Bosnia. Then it says: Bruno Busic, Ludvig Pavlovic, Vitezovi, Travnik Police Department, the 4th battalion of the military police in Vitez. So four units were mentioned. If you can see that just tell me what the date is.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the 16th of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So when an order is issued in this way, can you see any kind of subordination or resubordination amongst the above-mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who are they subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the unit that is operating in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But the order is issued by the commander of the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that, first and foremost, they are all subordinate to him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then, if you look at the order further, you will see whether there is coordination or subordination; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us not waste too much time. Jon Elford, witness Jon Elford, there is a document in the binder related to him. There is also an order issued by Blaskic, where he sends this order to the Viteska Brigade and the Zrinjski Brigade, and the 4th Battalion of the military police. So it's three units altogether. It's not really important which units they are. He says, explicitly in this order, that it enters into force immediately, and: "The commanders of the above-mentioned units shall be held responsible by me for the execution of this." Is this subordination or coordination?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, you mean coordination?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Because it was specifically said so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, it was part of the Elford binder and it was not registered under separate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's not waste any more time on this. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite. This document was not officially admitted by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. But we'll not spend any more time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In connection with this subject, just one question. The light artillery rocket division, you know that within the set-up of the operative zone of Central Bosnia there was such a unit?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Theoretically, according to the JNA concept, it belongs directly to the commander of the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it can also be given to the commander of the unit that is carrying out this particular action, depending on the nature of the operations concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: However, if nothing is said specifically, then it belongs to the organisation of the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we are going to play a tape to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you are not going to. You are going to ask the Trial Chamber whether you can do that. What is it you want to play? What is it that you want to play, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a tape here. Of course, I have a copy for the Prosecutor. It was recorded by the intelligence service of the HVO during the war. I have the transcripts as well. And I would like to ask the witness to do two things in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has it been admitted into evidence so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is something from the other side. Now, if you want to call evidence about it, you can do that, but you can't ask this witness about it. You are merely asking him to comment. Now, let's get onto something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Mr. President, I am just seeking permission for him to recognise whether he is the person speaking on this tape, to see whether the tape is authentic in terms of the persons whose voices are taped, because he is the only one who can recognise his own voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you made preparations for this to be played?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The technical booth has the tape, and we have the transcripts here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. But you are not to take a lot of time with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just suggest that we hear the first part -- only 10 or 15 seconds, so that the witness can say whether it is him or not. We are going to play the tape then, and I am going to put four or five brief questions related to the transcript to him, and that will have concluded what I had to do.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters now -- interpreters did not receive copies. The interpreters ask for a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask the director to put the sound on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the interpreters have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the transcript, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, who should see the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution should have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We don't need it for the other Defence. They have one. There were enough copies. Something was wrong. There were three for Judges --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Take one. We'll share.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sure there was. Something was missed out. Could we now play the tape, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Voice 1: Hello. Hi, how are you? What's up? Voice 2: Nothing. Voice 1: Everything is fine. Super - the only thing is that that Smajic from Bila called around 9.00 and he says that he heard that there was shooting in Travnik and he was only checking. The officer on duty in the Travnik headquarters said that there allegedly had been some skirmishes, something about flags or whatever, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, shall we continue listening to the tape or can you identify your voice?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could the director please play another conversation from this tape, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Voice 1: I don't know, it's not the flag. I don't know. It's a placard or something. I don't know. I don't know. Voice 2: Well, whatever, I can do it myself. I was born on my own. I grew up on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please hear the beginning of the second conversation, because that's where the tape is better, and then we are through.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Voice 1: How are things? Fine? Voice 2: Nothing. Voice 1: All quiet. What do you say, is there any shooting where you are? Voice 2: Says who? Voice 1: Nobody is shooting. Nobody is shooting. Voice 2: It's the usual thing, Ustashas are celebrating, you know. Voice 1: That means that nothing is going on? Voice 2: No, nothing. Voice 1: What about there. Voice 2: Nothing. Voice 1: Are you all right? Voice 2: Yes. Voice 1: When are you going to come here? Voice 2: Come on. Drop by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the third conversation, again your name is being used. It was not heard very well in the first conversation or the second conversation, we couldn't hear it well. Could you please listen to this carefully.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Voice 1: [Inaudible] called. Voice 2: Just wanted to see what was going on. Voice 1: What are you doing? Voice 2: Well, I've got a few men here. We're on duty, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, do you recognise your voice here or not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this into evidence, please, the tape and the transcript, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, what is there significant in it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me finish, Mr. Kovacic. What is significant in this document? Is there anything which you say this witness said or was said to him on which you rely?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It mostly shows -- indeed, there are a couple of incidents mentioned which are either very directly or indirectly within the picture of what the witness said, and I will be very, very brief on that. Indeed, out of those nine discussions, nine separate discussions, I would put the question on three or four just to identify whether the subject is what I would presume from the discussion in reality is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kalco, do you have the transcript in front of you? Just a brief question up there. It says, the first conversation, conversation 1, it is the person who is on duty at the headquarters with you, and I presume you must have called from outside to check --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in English. I don't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the transcript in Croatian. In the case of the first conversation, I think the witness said he didn't recognise his voice, as you allege it to be. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, the first conversation, there is mention of these flags here, and it doesn't really matter who said it. I believe it was you. But you talk about a flag, and you say, "Whoever did that, that is, hoisted it up, to take it down tomorrow, because we don't know what it is, whose it is. It's not a flag. It looks like a banner or something like that." To begin with, this is Eastertime, as the preceding sentence shows. Can we agree that it was Eastertime?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But do you remember that a huge, I mean an enormous flag -- I mean one was never seen before or after like that, huge, a huge green flag which was spread over the road next to the tyre repair shop at Bengir's in Stari Vitez, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you were not particularly happy about that either, were you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Why weren't you happy about it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because it was a provocation for the other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: By "the other people", you mean Croats?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, in Travnik a few days before that, some people got into fisticuffs and were injured because of the flags, and that is why you did not like that in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so, quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it was put up by some Mujahedins, by some extremists?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I do not know what you mean by "Mujahedin". To begin with, in Stari Vitez, there was not a single Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But perhaps it was some extremists who put up that flag?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Do you know if at that time a group of extremists -- sorry. Thank you. Now, the next conversation, I should also like to ask you something about that, conversation number 2 -- the third conversation, conversation number 3. I apologise. Conversation number 4, and you have it marked there, the fourth conversation. Here, at the bottom -- first, you are taking part in this conversation. Let us try to identify. This Neric who takes up the call, is that Hakija Dzalilovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neric was not a member of the BH army in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but is it Hakija Dzalilovic? Could you tell us who Neric is?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And towards the end of that conversation in some place somewhere, he says: "The fire place is gone. Kamin has left. When did he leave?" "He left an hour ago." And I should like to tell you that at 21.30 some days before that, a very popular restaurant in Vitez called Kamin was blown up. It was owned by somebody called Slavko Jukic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you -- does this person mean that Kamin?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is an objection, which I will hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is merely a comment. I really do not understand what are the conversations that the witness remembers having. Mr. Kovacic is addressing him as if he owned up to all these conversations. I think we should really establish which conversations the witness recognises as his own and accepts as his own amongst this large number of conversations which are shown here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So far, there is nothing of any significance in anything here. If there is and if necessary, it will have to be replayed to see whether the witness accepts it or not. But time is going, so let's move on. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In conversation 6, in the beginning we have a dialogue. Would you agree that it is you talking to Zahid Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No? You say it wasn't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Conversation 7, and this should be the conversation between you and Sifet Sivro, and you introduce yourself at the beginning. Will you please have a look at it to see what it's all about, and then I'll have one question. Are you referring to the disarmament of guards at the SPS, when somebody first tried to disarm some guards who were Croats, because at that time guards were still of mixed ethnicity, and after that the Ustasha, and it says here, their special troops came and disarmed the Muslim guards so that only Croat guards remained? Do you agree that the conversation is about that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know that it is that incident when the HVO came, but the HVO did come and disarm the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But before that, some Croats had been disarmed, and that is what then led on to --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody was disarmed by the BH army. They may have disarmed themselves so as to have a reason to do what they did then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then conversation 9, which is the last page, also in the beginning we hear clearly that it is you, because you give your name here, and you are asking for a certain Almir, and in the beginning you say, "Listen. We have some complaints from below that Besim Trako and Petak --" is this Senad Petak whom you mentioned yesterday and who was killed in the hotel on the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petak was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. The person who was with him, yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two Petaks. I do not really know who does this refer to. There were two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it the other brother, the one who is mentioned here? I can't find the right word, but were they rather quarrelsome persons, rather, short-tempered people before the war?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this shows -- this also says about some incident, that they seized somebody's pistol, didn't they, some Kulices [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yeah, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Your Honour, I have no further questions. [Interpretation] Mr. Kalco, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you asking for the transcripts to be put into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am. Sorry for that on the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you are talking about the admission of the transcript. Could we know the source of this transcript, and can the Prosecutor's office check the authenticity and the reliability of the translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Has the tape been given to the Prosecutor yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I just gave it. I gave it to the Registry, and I see they distributed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next point is this: Where does it come from, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It comes from the HVO municipality services in Vitez. From time to time, they were trying -- as you have heard in other testimonies, they have heard to listen to each other. Indeed, Witness Kalco mentioned that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit it on this basis: that, of course, the Prosecution can have the tape and can test it and can also, if need be, comment on the translation. But at the moment, it can be admitted. What's the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The tape is there. Your Honour, if I may just add, I'm planning to bring a witness, a technician who was working on that job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The audiotape will be number D65/2 and the transcript D65A/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. There is a matter I want to raise with Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Kovacic, you haven't challenged, in the witness's evidence -- and we should be plain what your case is about because you're obliged under the Rules, if you're going to dispute something, to put it to the witness -- first of all, in the October post office meeting, that Mr. Cerkez said that the municipality would burn down. Now, is it disputed that Mr. Cerkez said that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes, of course I dispute it, and I thought it clearly transpired from my question. Somebody said that there would be a fire, not a threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that was the item that followed that, we will get it straightened out. Mr. Kalco, it's suggested that somebody said that Mr. Cerkez didn't say the municipality would burn down but somebody said there would be a fire. Is that true or not? Just answer in a word, if you would.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not getting the interpretation. I'm not getting the interpretation. I can hear His Honour, but I am not getting the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question was this: Mr. Cerkez, you said, said at the October meeting in the post office that the municipality would burn down. It is suggested by the Defence that that was not said and that somebody said there would be a fire. Now, did somebody say there would be a fire or not? Would you tell us what the truth is?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is the former, that Vitez would be butchered and that the Bosniaks -- and that the blame would rest with the Bosniaks, that is the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the next matter, Mr. Kovacic, was this: that dealing with the 16th of April, the witness's evidence was that he had intercepted an order from Mario Cerkez to Marko Lujic to fire at religious objects at Kruscica. And Lujic subsequently asked for a break, said that they could have breakfast and that the guns could cool down. Now, is that conversation challenged?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That was challenged, Your Honour, because I asked the witness whether that was a discussion between Marko Lujic and his son, Mario Lujic. And the second -- that was the first document which I introduced to the witness, which shows that this person, Marko Lujic, was far beyond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a separate point. It's a separate point. So that I can understand your case, are you saying that this conversation was not with Mr. Cerkez, but was with somebody else? Is that the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Mario was another person. And if I may, Your Honour, this other person, Mario, was with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, you've heard what's suggested, that this was not a conversation with Mario Cerkez. Was it or not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was with -- between Mario and Marko Lujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, thank you, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I just want to refer on that subject witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all a matter of argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also challenge when we were talking about the meetings on or before 20 October. There are some mixed up on places and orders. Some persons were not here, but we do have already exhibits in the case, so it is obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. All that is a matter for comment. Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should simply like to comment on the witness's answer, looking at the transcript. Mr. President, when you asked if the conversation was between Mario Cerkez and another one, he said, "Yes, the conversation was between Mario and Marko Lujic." I believe it would be important to say that it was Mario Cerkez. It was said that Mario and Marko Lujic were talking, but to avoid any ambiguity, perhaps we should make it -- perhaps we should seek further precision, because the witness said only "Mario."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's perfectly fine. He was talking about his earlier evidence in which he said it was Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kalco.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I introduce myself, sir. My name is Stephen Sayers, and together with my colleague, Mr. Naumovski, we represent Dario Kordic. You've been asked a lot of questions today and yesterday, and I'll try to be as brief as I can, sir, and not go over territory --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, will you please slow down. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- and not go over territory that we have already been over, sir. The first question. You were the deputy commander of the 325th Mountain Brigade, the second in command to Sefkija Djidic; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was Sefkija Djidic's deputy. Sefkija Djidic was the commander of the TO staff of the municipality of Vitez, and I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in your direct testimony you gave some descriptions of the takeover, essentially, of the Vitez municipal government by the HVO. And I believe, sir, that that was on June the 20th of 1992, that that occurred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say anything about when the government was taken over, but it is that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this was -- this subject was not broached in the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You gave some testimony, sir, about dealings with the Croat political and military leaders in Vitez. And I believe that the people with whom you dealt principally were Ivica Santic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also dealt with Mr. Skopljak, both Pero and Marijan Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you also dealt with Mr. Anto Valenta; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And Mr. Valenta was a school teacher who taught at the high school in Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a teacher at the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And the leaders of the Muslim community were, I believe, Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic, for one; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe the chief of the military police was Mr. Saban Mahmutovic; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Civilian police. And then the military leaders were Mr. Djidic and yourself?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police was under our command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you have any meetings with Mr. Kordic in the spring or summer of 1992, and speak to him personally, so far as you are aware, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And just one final question on this, while -- before I move onto another subject. The negotiations between the Muslim side and the Croat side of the civil and military authorities in Vitez, if you like, continued on, really, until the outbreak of the war in April of 1993; isn't that right? Or at least the outbreak of the fighting between the Muslims and the Croats in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the 30th of April, when a military delegation of the HVO and a delegation of the BiH army came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Let me skip over some topics that I was going to cover, and let me turn straight to the blockade at Ahmici on the 18th of October 1992. There seems to be some uncertainty, sir, in the actual date of the blockade. Was it October the 18th, 1992, or the 19th or the 20th? Can you recall, at this remove of time, seven years or eight years afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was at that time. I do not have a document with me. I believe it was the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. This was the first time, though, would it be fair to say, Mr. Kalco, that a troop convoy had been stopped at gunpoint in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you say, sir, that the troop convoy was stopped, and it was stopped because it was carrying troops from a variety of municipalities to Novi Travnik. But isn't it true, sir, that Jajce had been under prolonged and heavy attack by the Bosnian Serb army forces at this time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Jajce was taken one of those days and that there was a disarray between the BiH army and HVO on one hand, because the Serbs were pushing forward so that both the ABiH and the HVO began retreating from Jajce. I said yesterday that the HVO's objective was, because they had the explosives factory in Vitez, and they also wanted to take the ammunition factory in Novi Travnik, because of the artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You would agree, though, that the town of Jajce actually was captured by the forces of the Bosnian Serb army about ten days after the blockade had been erected at Ahmici; isn't that right? I don't think there is any dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there were some indications, there were some signs, and the units were withdrawing from Jajce, were pulling out of Jajce, because, of course, they could not pull out overnight. It was clear that Jajce was about to fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What you are telling us, then, Mr. Kalco, if I understand you correctly, is that the units of the Muslim forces were withdrawing from Jajce because they saw the writing on the wall, so to speak, and that the HVO was doing the same thing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. Both forces. Yes. Except that the HV, that in Jajce the command was in the hands of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And, Mr. President, I just draw the Trial Chamber's attention to Exhibit 151/1, the entry for October 31st, 1992, which actually contains a date that Jajce fell. Let me just move onto another point, sir. You related to us that instructions had been received by your headquarters to erect the blockades at Stari Bila and at Ahmici shortly before they were actually erected; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I think and you said in your statement, five years ago, that Ahmici was selected because it was a natural choke point; the HVO forces could not pass from any other direction, if they were stopped there. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite. Because that is the boundary between the Vitez and the Busovaca municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you only went to Ahmici after the fighting had already occurred; is that right, Mr. Kalco?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the fighting ended. No, not during the fighting, but when the passions abated somewhat, it is then that they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's what I thought you said. Now, let me turn your attention to the first of the four items that I would like to concentrate upon particularly. You mentioned some negotiations that occurred between the two parties on the opposite sides of the dispute, let's say. And in your statement, five years ago, you said that on October the 20th, at about 7.00 a.m., you received a telephone call from Ivica Santic, requesting permission to come to the army headquarters, your army headquarters, for a meeting. All these years later, sir, do you actually recall what the date was, or not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. This was the 20th. Not at 7.00, but at 7.00 in the evening, at 1900 hours. Not in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And you are certain it was on October the 20th, 1992, right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. And, as I understand it, sir, a delegation of people arrived in your headquarters consisting of, amongst others, Ivica Santic, Pero Skopljak, Mr. Marijan Skopljak, and Mr. Cerkez; is that accurate to say?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Santic, Ivica was there, and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No others?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, were there any representatives of the civilian side, from the Muslims? Mr. Kajmovic, for example, was he there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kajmovic was there, Mujezinovic. There were some others from the Muslim civilian authorities and from the command of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If this is the meeting that I think it is, Mr. Kalco, the Trial Chamber's already heard a lot of evidence about this, and I don't want to spend too much time on this. But let me just ask you, was Mr. Kaknjo there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And two other names, Mr. Sivro Bahtija and Mr. Salkic Suad, were there too, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure about Sivro, but Suad Salkic was a member of the BiH army staff, and he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And was it the next day, sir, that you received a call from Dr. Franjo Tibolt, trying to act as a mediator between the two parties, a nascent to the dispute?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the same day, after the meeting, we heard from Dr. Tibolt that a meeting should be organised between the army and the HVO at the medical centre. And we came to that meeting, as I already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you indeed, Mr. Kalco. So as I understand it, the chronology is that you had the meeting with Mr. Santic and Mr. Cerkez first, and then after that meeting you received a call from Dr. Tibolt, in another attempt at mediation, and that was followed by yet a third meeting that you had with Mr. Cerkez, following which the fighting broke out; is that accurate to say?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. And the meeting that you had with Mr. Cerkez and -- at which Mr. Djidic was present, that occurred at 6.00 a.m., the morning after the first two conversations that you've talked about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, sir, the paragraph 23 of the offer of proof that you apparently reviewed and signed yesterday, contains a reference to a telephone conversation that supposedly occurred between Ivica Santic and Mr. Kordic. There was no mention of that conversation at all in your statement five years ago. Do you have a clear recollection of Mr. Santic making a telephone call to someone, and him telling you who that telephone call was being made to or not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that Ivica Santic, as president of the HVO and mayor of Vitez, called. And after that conversation, he said that he had talked to Mr. Kordic, who was in Novi Travnik, and he received orders that they had to be released, that units were to go from Busovaca to Novi Travnik. Those were his orders, because he was the man in charge in Central Bosnia, Boban and him. And he was in charge of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sir, as the deputy commander, did you report that to your intelligence officer, Mr. Nihad Rebihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether any contemporaneous note or memorandum was made of that discussion, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A note was made about the talk between the two components. I don't know where the note is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Do you know whether that note was passed up your chain of command to the 3rd Corps in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. But since we don't have that note, the only thing we have is your recollection of a conversation that occurred eight years ago, or seven-and-a-half years ago. Now, how long did that conversation last, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Let the witness comment on that. It said that this all happened eight years ago. Do you remember it, Mr. Kalco?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember well, because I didn't know who he had been talking to. Mr. Santic said that he called Mr. Kordic, and I remember that Mr. Kordic said that he was in Novi Travnik. That's for sure; one hundred per cent. If he talked to someone else and just told us this, that's another matter. That's not for me to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's time now for a break. If you are moving onto the next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have just a couple of comments about that conversation, but we can take a break now, Your Honour. It's just as good as any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And how long do you expect to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As I related yesterday, I would think not more than half an hour total. I would anticipate, realising that we have other witnesses here, by 11.15 or 11.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Mr. President. May I have this pause to let the witness examine this transcript of the tape, and then say whatever he has to say about this, because he will be leaving today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, he can do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I just say that there is a fairly urgent matter that we need to take up following the conclusion of this witness's testimony and before the next witness testifies. That will take about five minutes, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, let us continue on chronologically over the items that you talked about, insofar as they concern Mr. Kordic, anyway. And as I said, I'll try not to detain you here not more than another 15 or 20 minutes. Now, you made no mention of this conversation between Mr. Santic and Mr. Kordic in your statement five years ago. The first time that we heard about it was yesterday. Did you actually see Mr. Santic make the telephone call that you've testified about, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it, because the telephone was on the desk. There were 12 of us sitting there, and I saw that somebody made a call to somebody. We did not know whom. And after the conversation, he said what he said. I don't want to repeat what I already have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The point is, though, and I just want to underscore this, you said during your direct examination that you don't know what was said, you weren't able to hear the conversation, and that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite. Nobody could hear -- nobody could overhear the conversation. Santic was talking. He was the only one who could hear, and he told us about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's move on to the next point. You do recall attending a meeting on the 22nd of October, or shortly after the fighting broke out at Ahmici, with the politicians in Vitez and your commanding officer, Mr. Djidic, as well as representatives from UNPROFOR, Captain Sajmon Elis, I believe, and a representative of the ECMM, Mr. Anders Levinsen. Do you remember that meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it would be fair to say, wouldn't it, and I think you'll agree with this, that Mr. Kordic was not involved in any way in the negotiations that led to the reduction in tensions following the fighting in Ahmici and the resolution of that situation that had occurred just a few days before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite right, he did not, because we talked to relevant military and civilian authorities in the municipality of Vitez, and Mr. Kordic comes from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. You did not consider Mr. Kordic to be one of the relevant military or civil authorities in the region, in your municipality, did you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not consider him to be that in Vitez itself. But in the region, yes, we did perceive him as such, as he was the main personality in Central Bosnia, from Kresevo to Kiseljak down to Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever spoken to Mr. Kordic, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I already said that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you gave some brief testimony about members of a unit that wore oak leaf patches. I believe they were called the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it's true, sir, that this brigade came to Vitez, I believe you said in your statement five years ago, around September of 1992 and caused all kinds of problems; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was when they arrived that the problems culminated in Vitez, as against the previous period, because they were teasing, provoking people, beating people. When out in restaurants and coffee shops, their behaviour was improper, and I suppose that they were the ones, with HVO extremists in Vitez itself, who were responsible for the blowing up of Muslim facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Just three final points with respect to this brigade. Your troops reported to you that several members of this brigade were actually killed in the fighting at Ahmici on the 20th of October, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had received reports that some HVO soldiers had been killed, but we did not know which brigade it was or who were those soldiers; that is, whether they came from Vitez, or perhaps from Ludvig Pavlovic, or perhaps some other unit. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You said in your statement five years ago, on page 4, that: "Members of the Territorial Defence at Ahmici told me that some of the dead HVO soldiers at Ahmici on 20 October, 1992, were members of this brigade. They knew this because of the oak leaf patch on their uniforms." Now, does that help you remember -- I know it's a long time later, sir, but does that help you remember whether there were members of this brigade that your troops reported to have been killed in the fighting in Ahmici on that date?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I said in my statement, but I did not see any one of them. And I believed what I was told by the soldiers, by men of the BiH army who had been at that front. I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No criticism intended at all. Following this incident, though, you insisted to your immediate superior, or the second in command of the 3rd Corps, Colonel Merdan, that all HVO units, not from Vitez, had to leave the municipality. That was one of the conditions upon which you insisted during the ceasefire negotiations and peace negotiations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.
