utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And they did in fact leave the municipality of Vitez around the 25th of December 1992; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Towards the end of the year. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, were you aware that there had been an outbreak of fighting between HVO or Croat forces and Muslim forces in the Busovaca municipality in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The refugees from Kovacevac arrived in Vitez from Vranjska, and then they were transferred to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In analysing the tensions that gradually increased between the Muslim residents of the Lasva Valley and the Croat residents, sir, were you aware that there had been a series of executions and murders outside of Busovaca in the villages of Dusina, and the villages around Kacuni, Oseliste, Gusti Grab, Donja Polje, places like that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear those stories, but I wasn't showing much interest for them because they were outside of my area of responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So let me move on immediately, sir. You don't know very much about that fighting at all; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you talked about artillery assets and artillery commanders. You became aware yourself of the arrival of certain pieces of artillery ordnance in the Vitez area in the spring of 1993, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, you were aware that two 155-millimetre howitzers had arrived in the area, one based at Mali Mosunj, the quarry; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Prahulje, Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Could you give us your best estimate of the distance between the quarry at Mosunj and the second location that you've identified, Prahulje near Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, would you agree that the quarry at Mali Mosunj is about two kilometres away from Prahulje?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thereabouts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one question, sir, in connection with the testimony that you gave surrounding Mr. Miroslav Bralo. Were you aware that Mr. Bralo had actually been imprisoned at the Kaonik military detention facility and that he was in gaol in March of 1993, as a result of the unfortunate murder of Mr. Esad Salko -- Salkic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that he had been detained, but he spent a very short time in prison. He moved about. He was quite free. And I presume he was allowed to go free after the investigation. And I really don't feel like talking about Bralo any more, because he used to boast that he had killed over 50 Bosniaks, and so on and so forth. The gentlemen in the HVO know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, I don't blame you in the least. The last question I have on the subject of this unsavoury individual is you never saw him at liberty yourself in March of 1993, did you, with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him in Vitez on a couple of occasions in a luxury car. He was loaded at the time, when people did not work. And when we survived only owing humanitarian aid, he was loaded with German marks, he was spending Croatian dinars. I don't know where he got them. But I know that he wasn't poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. I appreciate you may have seen him, but did you see him in March of 1993, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was March. After that event, I did see him. It was after those incidents that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing that up, sir. Now, in connection with the testimony that you gave about the alleged assassination attempt upon Mr. Darko Kraljevic. Do you know whether any reports were made of that event, and your conclusions to your intelligence officer, Mr. Rebihic, or passed on up your chain of command to the 3rd Corps in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a report was made, a proper, good report, and sent to the 3rd Corps. Where that report is now, I don't know. I suppose it is somewhere in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. It would be fair to say, sir, that you, as the second in command, wanted to ensure with your intelligence officer, Mr. Rebihic, that accurate, contemporaneous records were made of any significant event in your area of responsibility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite. That is right. So that people should know who did what, where they did it, what are the consequences of that, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And, in fact, that was one of your duties and one of the duties of your intelligence officer, Mr. Rebihic; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was his superior, and he did his job when I ordered him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, with respect to the kidnapping of Commander Zivko Totic on the 15th of April. You were aware of that incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was attending the celebration of the army day in Zenica, and that is when I heard that. But it is again outside our area, that is the territory of the Vitez municipality. It is Zenica, so that is where I heard about it, at that particular meeting, at the celebration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you able to see the televised press conference that was held in the morning of the 15th of April, showing video footage of the circumstances under which Commander Totic had been kidnapped and his four escorts slaughtered?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of it, yes. I don't really remember any detail, but I did see some of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you remember seeing Mr. Kordic give a speech during that press conference at all, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let me just tell you, if I may. The press conferences held by Mr. Kordic could not be followed in Zenica, could not be taped in Zenica, so that we tape-recorded all these press conferences and sent tapes to the 3rd Corps in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Any time that there was a significant press conference containing either political or military information of interest to your commander and you, you would make a videotape of the conference and send it up the chain of command in due course to your superiors at the 3rd Corps; is that accurate to say?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kalco, do you know a gentleman by the name of Fuad Berbic, the former TO commander in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. We served in the JNA together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was a professional soldier; is that fair to say as well?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me. What did he do, sir, for a profession, for his job?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a commander of the unit in Ahmici --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and member of the local staff in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say that he was extremely critical of the way that the entire barricade incident had been organised in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I know. Perhaps, but I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on to one question concerning the fighting that broke out in Stari Vitez on the 16th of April. It's true, isn't it, that in the first wave of the fighting that broke out there, your forces killed 11 HVO soldiers and suffered three fatalities on your side?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, we had three dead on the first day of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were HVO soldiers killed. I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your statement five years ago, sir, maybe your memory was fresher then than it is now, but let me just read you a statement on page 9 and see if it refreshes your recollection. You said there: "In the first attack, three BiH soldiers were killed, but we killed 11 HVO soldiers." Does that help you remember what happened in the first attack there on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, true. We knew that it was about 11, and we also think that there were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just a couple of questions in connection with the Stari Vitez truck bomb explosion. Are you sure of the date of that explosion, sir, whether it was the 18th, or the 19th, or is that not clear to you at this point?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: True, at half past 5.00, and it was a Sunday. On Friday, they attacked Vitez. The 16th, 17th, that is, Friday, Saturday, and then it was Sunday, so it must have been the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was the electricity still working at that time, sir, on the 18th or the 19th when the truck bomb exploded; yes?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was still electricity on the 18th or, rather, on the 16th and the 17th, and after the explosion, it was cut off, there was no more electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you related certain comments made by Mr. Kordic allegedly in a television programme that evening. Let me just ask you, were you the only person to see that programme, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How can he answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There may have been other people with him in the room, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a different matter. Did you see it alone or were there others with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was at the command. I don't know how many officers of the command were there. But since there was no electricity, we had a battery-powered TV set, and we would charge batteries for our stations all the time. After that, it was 15 or 16 days without electricity after that, so that we had our radio stations, and we had light, and we had also a TV set, that is, so we could watch it and listen to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, were you alone in the room where the TV programme was broadcast or were there other people there with you, and if so, who were they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's answered that question.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know the names of anybody who might have been there or not, Mr. Kalco?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have it written down here in that notebook of mine. I know that the signals men were with me, two or three of them, and I could not say right now who else from the staff members was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just two lines of questions. First, did you make a videotape of this television broadcast and send it up your chain of command, as was your normal practice?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. We recorded that conversation as well. We could not send it up immediately because it was closed. However, when negotiations took place on the 30th of June or, rather, on the 30th of April, when the ceasefire was in place, we gave this tape to our officers, who handed it over to the 3rd Corps in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, sir. Now a follow-up question from that. Have you ever seen a videotape of that press conference, or news announcement, or whatever it was from that day to this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have. And when did you see that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we taped it, then I watched it again. We watched it again, the command. We watched this tape to see whether it turned out all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I take it that the tape quality was good, you could hear what people were saying.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the image quality was good as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you're quite correct, Mr. Kalco. In the question that I asked you, that was the correct answer. But let me ask you this: From the time that you turned over the videotape that you made to your superior officers in the 3rd Corps after June of 1993, until today have you seen that videotape or that programme rerun on TV?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to another subject. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, is it disputed that Dario Kordic said that the ammunition depot had been activated, there would be more explosions of the kind, and the ABiH members should surrender?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It is disputed, Mr. President, yes. My client has no recollection of making any such a statement on the 19th and really no recollection of being informed that there had been an explosion in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Kalco, let me turn to the conversation that you had with Colonel Blaskic on the 30th of April. Now, you told us yesterday that General Petkovic was in attendance with Colonel Blaskic at this meeting that you had with them. But in your statement five years ago, you said that it was actually Colonel Blaskic, Colonel Filipovic, and Commander Totic. Let me just read you a statement that you made. On page 10, it says: "On 30 April 1993, I attended a meeting in Stari Vitez with Blaskic, Filipovic, and Totic." Let me just ask you, sir, was Commander Totic present at this meeting or wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I just refer the Court to Exhibit 79/1, Annex C, which shows that Commander Totic was not, in fact, released from custody in Zenica, as a captive of the Mujahedin, until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's all a matter of comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Maybe I should put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Mr. Kalco, that, in fact, Commander Totic was not present at this meeting because he was still a captive of the Mujahedin in Zenica and was not released until May the 17th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was at the meeting in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's as best you remember it, sir, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to answer that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you, in conformity with your normal practice, make contemporaneous notes and memoranda, or memorandum, about this conversation that you'd had with Colonel Blaskic and send it up your chain of command to the 3rd Corps in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, there was Sefer Halilovic, there was Rasim Delic, there was Vehbija Karic. They made notes. I only made a report for internal purposes, and I informed the staff in Vitez. And they probably made a report for the 3rd Corps or, rather, the Supreme Command of the BiH army. We didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. You would agree that it was a very important event for you, to receive visits from the Commander in Chief of the Armija of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Commander in Chief of the HVO; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. And we thought that the ceasefire achieved then would stay on, and that there would be no war. And it went on only for a few days, and then the conflict started again. Fortunately, people were released from prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you, what is true, sir? Is it that Colonel Blaskic, Colonel Filipovic, and Commander Totic were present at this meeting, as you said five years ago, or is it true that General Petkovic, General Halilovic, and Colonel Blaskic were present at this meeting, as you said yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. When I stated this five years ago, it was true. And also what I said yesterday, that's it. There was this broader meeting. Not to repeat all of that. At any rate, Petkovic led the HVO team, and Sefer Halilovic was the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the BiH army, and he led the army delegation. It was the three of them, and I was the fourth one from Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me pass onto my two final topics. Firstly, you gave some testimony about seeing someone that you identified as Mr. Kordic on the 8th of August of 1993. Now, sir, you were actually standing inside a building in Stari Vitez, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a building. It was ruins, the remains of a building that had been shelled. I was touring the lines, and in the village of Krcevine I saw what I spoke of yesterday, and that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, how far away were the ruins of this house from the southern bank of the Lasva River, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about 500 or 600 metres. You can see it well with binoculars. You can even discern features, faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps I misunderstood you, sir. Did you say that you were about 500 metres away from the southern bank of the Lasva River, at the place that you were standing, looking for your binoculars?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The distance between myself and this HVO line in Krcevine was 500 to 600 metres, approximately. That is the northern side, Krcevine. And I was on the southern side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. In other words, you were on the southern side of the Lasva River, and Krcevine, as the Court can see from the map, is over on the northern bank of the Lasva River, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or, to put it better, I was on the right bank of the Lasva River, and they were on the left bank of the Lasva River.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you couldn't hear a word that was being said, could you, during the --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No. No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And you say that Mr. Kordic was in plain view, along with all the other military commanders, looking through your optical instruments at them 500 metres or so away; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in plain view of anybody who was standing in the area that you were, with optical instruments as well?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you also gave some testimony about Mr. Kordic appearing on TV later that night or the next day. Did you make a videotape of that news conference or announcement, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we recorded that too. And we kept it in our headquarters until the ceasefire. After the ceasefire, we gave it to the 3rd Corps in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I take it, that you also made a contemporaneous note or a memorandum or a report yourself, or your intelligence officer did, and that that was passed up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My intelligence officer made a report based on the data that I gave him. He made a report to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Final subject, sir. Helicopters. You gave some testimony on this subject. Isn't it true that the helicopters that you saw were generally small, non-cargo helicopters, the first being a Galeb model, and the second being a French Gazelle model helicopter; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were small helicopters for the most part. They had two or three flights one evening, even four. Sometimes they would actually land, and in other places they would just parachute the parcels that they were transporting. We benefited from that too, because sometimes we got the parcels containing ammunition and other things that were meant for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think you said that yesterday. Here is my final question. In connection with the assault that was launched upon Stari Vitez in the middle of July of 1993, the 18th, I think you said, isn't it true that the bulldozer that -- or the converted bulldozer that you described, was actually halted, having been struck by a shoulder-launched missile fired by one of your troops fired from Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. Yes. Thank God it was hit. Had it not been hit, I wonder what would have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you indeed, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, so that we understand your case, is it disputed that Mr. Kordic was on the front line on the 8th of August 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I enquired of my client yesterday on that subject, Mr. President. And if you'll bear with me for just 30 seconds. He believes that the incident that Mr. Kalco may have been referring to is a visit that he made to that village, many civilians had been killed in the village, and he came to visit their families. And what was related as to what was supposedly said on TV the next day is disputed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Before I ask you some questions, in order to specify things, I should like to go back to the tape that was produced this morning. Mr. Kalco, during the break you had an opportunity to go through the contents of the conversations which appear on that tape. There were nine conversations, all in all. And you recognised your voice in five of these conversations, and they are one, two, three, eight, and nine. And you put your signature, as I asked you, to each one of these conversations. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: A photocopy of this transcript, in the Bosniak language, has been submitted to the Chamber, together with the signature of the witness. It is D65/1, and it was submitted to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It should be added to the exhibit which we already have. And I'll be reminded of the number. I think -- was it 65/2? That document which the witness has signed, if you would hand it in now, can be marked D65/2.A. If you'll hand it in, unless there is something you want to ask about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two questions regarding these conversations, but not as to the document as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the document go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The copy in question is the one which was handed to us by the Defence a moment ago. We do not have any other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, is that your signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Hand it in now, please, to the Registry, and it can be marked. Is there any difficulty about marking it D65/2.A?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The transcript was marked D65/A.2. Maybe mark this one D65/B.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's get it marked -- no, don't hand it to the witness. Hand it to the Registry, please. Now, Mr. Kovacic, what point can you be made to make?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, microphone for Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to point out, since it was not really standard procedure, but we do accept the discussion -- the taped discussion under number 4 was recognised by the witness during his cross-examination, so he either did not recognise that when going through those materials or he changed his mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is the one, if I may remind, where I put the questions about restaurants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, the conversations which were shown to you this morning, could you tell us, what were the telephone lines on which they could have been recorded?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: PTT telephones, regular PTT telephones, because the post office was held by the HVO and they probably recorded all of it. Well, of course they recorded it. I'm sure that even now they have my own telephone bugged at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And these conversations, there were nine of them, and you recognised five of them. Do you have any idea as to when they were taped? Was it over a long period of time or was it much shorter?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mostly the second half of 1992 and until the conflict in 1993. There were probably other conversations as well, but they are not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And the telephone lines was the line that you used from your office, that is, from the headquarters of the Territorial Defence; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. We had that telephone line, and we also had a radio link with the units that were on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. This is all regarding telephone lines. Yesterday, Mr. Kovacic asked you some questions about BH army soldiers who were going to the front against the Serbs, and it is this subject that I should like to address now. The BH army soldiers, at the time that we are referring to, that is, in '92/'93, did they all -- did each one of them have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. When we ended our conflicts with the HVO, we had 70 per cent of weapons, and when we finished the war with the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we had armed the entire army, at least we in Vitez, because we did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In other words, as the soldiers were coming back on a leave, on a week leave, as you said, did they bring their weapons back home with them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that only officers brought their weapons home, their rifles, and the soldiers who had their own pistols. All other weapons remained at the front line for the shift that was taking over the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Mr. Kalco, how many soldiers from the Vitez municipality, and especially the Vitez Brigade, were deployed on the front against Serbs in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one detachment, 100 to 200 men from Vitez; up to 200 men, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In April 1993; we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you know where they were deployed? I'm referring to the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably at Vlasic, in the Turbe/Vlasic area, over there. I don't know that they were anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did those soldiers come back to Vitez prior to the 16th of April, or in the days following the 16th of April, or did they stay at the Serb front?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They returned before the conflict, before the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: If I understand you, the 16th of April, 1993, on that day there were no more Vitez soldiers or soldiers from the Vitez Brigade on the Serb front any longer.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Kovacic also mentioned various units which were in the Vitez municipality, and he asked several questions about the military police. Was there a military police unit within the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every brigade had its own platoon of the military police. It consisted of at least 30 men and perhaps even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the military police unit in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the brigade. He had a commander of this military police unit, but he was the commander of all units within his brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In other words, Mr. Mario Cerkez was the superior officer of the military police unit which was part of his brigade?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that that was not the issue on the direct, that we are entering a new area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's keep moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, that was the day of the car bomb explosion. You confirmed today that it was, indeed, the 18th of April. After the explosion, you said that it was followed by an infantry attack?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an attack coming from all sides, from the eastern side, from the new part of Vitez, from the garages, from Princip, from the church, across the Lasva River from the Rajic/Bilic houses; that is to say, an all-out attack coming from all sides of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And this attack practically came on top of the car bomb explosion, did it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. That is when people were so frightened, they didn't know what was going on. That's when the infantry attack started, along with artillery preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In view of the scope of the attack, the Vitezovi could not have launched it by themselves alone?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think had they had five times as many men as they did have, they could not have done it on their own. There had to be other units involved as well. May I mention another thing in this context to the Court. If one looks at the entire conflict or, rather, the encirclement of Vitez, there were these so-called improvised bombs. We called them babies. They were made of weapons that were highly destructive. They were filled with iron scraps and then concrete too. So after they would explode, soldiers or the population in general would be wounded terribly, all of those who would be injured by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You also spoke of the second attack on the 18th of July, 1993, on Stari Vitez, when there were at least 27 dead on the HVO side, and this also was a coordinated attack, that is, different forces of the HVO in Vitez, including those of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. From Princip, the Vitezovi; from the garages --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You don't have to go into details. I only wanted you to confirm it. Mr. Borislav Josic, who took over 12 bodies, also came from the Vitez Brigade, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was an officer, and he took over the dead HVO soldiers from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And as for Miroslav Bralo, he was also mentioned before, this morning he was shown documents according to which he had been taken into custody and detained, at least for a while. To your knowledge, was Mr. Bralo ever brought to court and did he receive a sentence for the murder of Mr. Salkic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no trial, because he would be detained and then he would be released, and I abide by the statement I made yesterday and today. I don't want to repeat it, once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: As to the documents that were shown to you this morning, you noted that Mr. Bralo was indicated as the person appearing in the military registry of the municipal headquarters in Vitez. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. That's right. You are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, I think we must bring this examination to an end. This witness has been giving evidence for more than a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a new document that was adduced this morning, Mr. President. I thought we should go through that, but I shall turn to some other points.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers also asked you some questions this morning and in this regard. You were asked as to the date when the meeting at the post office took place. And was it the 19th or the 20th of October? And you said that the attack on Ahmici had taken place in the morning of the 20th of October, and that the meeting at the post office preceded it. So it must have been the 19th of October, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were shown a document, which was Colonel Blaskic's order on the 16th of January 1993, and that was 811, and it said that Ludvig Pavlovic -- I think you were shown this morning. You were shown the document this morning. It is of the 16th of January 1993. Colonel Blaskic issues orders to this brigade saying that it is -- which means that it was still in Vitez, on the 16th of January 1993, and this brigade was still in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at that point in time it was leaving Vitez, in January. In January 1993. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But you recognise that that unit could still have been in the region of Vitez on the 16th of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KALCO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kalco, that concludes your evidence, and you are free to go. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Very briefly, if I might just hand up to the Trial Chamber some documents that were delivered to us today. They concern Witness AO, a witness who testified, I believe, yesterday and the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably better at this stage if I can interrupt, to deal with this in private session at this stage, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It can certainly be dealt with in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go into private session, is this a matter which has to be dealt with now, or can it be dealt with when we at least finish the next witness, who needs to get away?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, it can be dealt with after that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll see what this is and consider that then. Let's call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to this next witness, we received an offer of proof late last night, and without prejudice to our position that generally this isn't the right thing to do, we would not be adverse to having the witness statement taken as read, in the interests of saving time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kovacic, are you involved in this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, we don't have objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am grateful for that. And I will confine myself, I think, to three topics, which I'll ask for some clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. As far as timing is concerned, we started this session rather later than normal, so we'll go on till 12.40. We'll adjourn for lunch until ten minutes past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Brigadier Hayes, you have signed a summary of your evidence, I think, prepared over the last day or so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And do you sign it on the basis that it's an accurate account of evidence that you could give?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That summary sets out your involvement in affairs into which we are inquiring, starting on the 6th of April of 1993, when you went to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 11th of April, when there was the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Followed by the incident at Ahmici, which perhaps changed the focus of attention, and led to your making one or two trips in that area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could a pause be made, please, between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the interpreters are asking you to pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just deal briefly, please, if you may, with the 8th of May joint statement by Mladic and Halilovic about the ceasefire. Just in a sentence or so, what was the effect of all of that?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: This was a meeting in the airport at Sarajevo where a Bosnia-wide ceasefire was signed between General Mladic and General Halilovic, a bilateral ceasefire. The result of that was an increase in fighting in Central Bosnia and particularly in Mostar. And it was the perception of the headquarters that I worked in that the Croats perceive the possibility of some modified peace plan for Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a result of which they were intent on seizing as much land as they could get. Any ceasefire at that time froze the front lines where they were, and consequently, if you were not in possession of a certain piece of ground, you would lose it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A brief comment on paragraph 10, the mixed military working group meeting on the 9th of June. And just explain what the role or the relationship was between Petkovic and Siber, and why?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: On the 9th of June, we had a mixed military working group meeting in Kiseljak at the United Nations headquarters there. General Petkovic was representing the HVO as the commander in chief, Colonel Siber, or Mr. Siber, was representing the Bosnian army. General Petkovic refused to negotiate with Mr. Siber, on the grounds that it was not a Bosnian army, and Siber, therefore as a Croat, could not represent that army. It was, in General Petkovic's eyes, a Muslim army. This was not unusual. The same attitude would quite often be taken by the Serbs if Colonel Divjak represented the Bosnian army. The result of it was that the negotiations could not be held, and we had to delay until General Delic came from Sarajevo to represent the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you now, please, to just give us a summary of your involvement in the Convoy of Joy, so far as in particular it involved the defendant, Dario Kordic, your judgement of his involvement in that, and also Anto Valenta.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: When General Delic arrived in Kiseljak, the meeting took place between Petkovic and himself, with the aim of establishing a bilateral ceasefire between the Croats and the Muslims, to build on the ceasefire that had been agreed between Serbs and Muslims on the 8th of May. We had heard about the Convoy of Joy; a convoy organised by a Muslim from Tuzla to bring supplies from the coast up to Tuzla, that were needed in the Tuzla enclave. General Petkovic undertook to try to secure the safe passage of the convoy through Vitez. We believed that there could be some trouble at Vitez. He contacted the HVO in Vitez by using HVO communications from their own headquarters in Kiseljak, but was unable to secure the safe passage of the convoy. He asked if United Nations could escort the convoy, but it was explained to him that as it was not an UNHCR sponsored convoy, we were not able to do so. He left Kiseljak to go to Mostar at the end of the meeting, and undertook to go personally to Vitez to try and secure the safe passage of the convoy. He failed to do this. And my opinion was that although he was the commander-in-chief of the HVO, his authority within the Vitez pocket was somewhat limited. Shortly after this, we heard that the convoy had in fact been attacked, some drivers had been killed, some vehicles had been hijacked, and the rest of the convoy had been scattered. The British Battalion in Vitez was trying to gather the remains of the convoy together into a quarry where they could guard them, and then escort them out of the pocket. In view of what had happened, this seemed to be the only sensible course of action, which would avoid any further loss of life. I decided that I would go to Vitez to see the situation for myself. I travelled there, and on arrival, I was briefed by the British Battalion on the situation. During this briefing, the Muslim who had organised and was leading the convoy was brought into the British camp, and I had a chance to speak to him. He was a man on the verge of a breakdown. It was clear to me that he had been extremely shocked by what had happened to the convoy, and that it had been totally unexpected. He was very distressed. He was very emotional. I went out onto the ground to see the situation for myself, and at the eastern end of the Vitez pocket I came across a series of vehicles that were being hijacked by uniformed Croats, HVO and police. At some point during this time, I met with Ambassador Thebault. Nobody on the ground, on the Croat side, appeared to be making any attempt to stop the hijacking. I asked who had the authority to prevent this sort of action, and I was directed to Dario Kordic. After about an hour, we found Dario Kordic in a wood yard, which is to the west end of the pocket. Ambassador Thebault and I spoke to him. We complained about what had happened to the convoy, and that the -- it had been attacked and that vehicles had been looted, and were still being looted. Kordic said that he was doing his very best to gather the convoy together, that he had about 80 vehicles that he needed to collect. In fact, I think eventually about 40 vehicles were retrieved from the convoy. Despite what he was saying, I got the impression that he was not being entirely truthful, and that he was not actually doing his best to stop the looting or collect the convoy remnants together, despite the fact that he very clearly did have authority within the pocket and, in my opinion, it was within his gift to have stopped the looting and collected the convoy together. We went back out onto the ground to go to the quarry where the vehicles were being gathered under the guard of the British Battalion. Anto Valenta was leading us to this quarry. On the way, we passed a line of vehicles which were quite clearly from the convoy. They were being looted by HVO soldiers. In my opinion, it would have been impossible for Mr. Valenta not to have seen what was happening, but he chose not to stop. Rather, he ignored it and carried on. Ambassador Thebault and myself stopped. We managed to prevent the looting, but unfortunately there were no more Muslim drivers who could collect the vehicles and take them to the quarry. We continued on to the quarry. We saw the situation there. And towards the end of that day, we again saw Dario Kordic and again complained about what was happening on the ground. Once more, he assured us that he was doing his best to collect the convoy together, but once more I was less than reassured that he was actually doing his best. I felt that his attitude and the attitude of the HVO in the Vitez pocket was one of indifference to the convoy, to the individuals, to the hijacking of the vehicles, and to the looting that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just three matters of detail. So far as Petkovic is concerned, did you think his efforts were genuine?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And should a general at that level have been in a position to have control over people at the level of the Vitez pocket?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Certainly, as commander-in-chief of the HVO, he should have been able to have authority over the HVO in the Vitez pocket. They should have reacted to the orders and instructions that he gave them. And I have no doubt that he was genuinely trying to secure the safe passage of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your talks with Kordic, did he identify anyone as superior, as subordinate, or collateral to him who had either been responsible for stopping the convoy or who would have had authority and power to release it?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: He did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the occasion when you went there with Valenta in broad daylight?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: It was. It would have been at about 2000. It did not get dark until 2200 at that time of year in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other things. Paragraph 18. On the 19th of June of 1993, were there some Muslim families, who were close to the U.N. camp in Kiseljak, who were evicted?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: There were. There was a certain amount of intimidation of Muslim families in the town of Kiseljak going on at the time. This family came from houses that were opposite the camp, very close by. It was a group of women, children, and at least one youth. Numbers were in the region of ten, I believe. We admitted them to the camp because they were too frightened to return to their homes. They stayed in the medical centre, where we accommodated them. Vinko Lucic, who was the HVO-UNPROFOR liaison officer in Kiseljak, whom we knew quite well, came to speak to them to try to persuade them to return to their homes, but they refused to go. They were too frightened. We subsequently transported them to Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, on your summary and on the question of linkage, can you tell us just a little about the Muslim hospital and the incident there in August and September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Towards the end of August and beginning of September, General Briquemont, as commander of the UNPROFOR forces in Bosnia, was attempting to negotiate further ceasefires in the evacuation of wounded civilians from certain locations. I was in East Mostar at the time. I visited the Muslim hospital that was there, and having seen the conditions, I went to the HVO headquarters on the west bank to try to negotiate the evacuation of the wounded from this hospital. The evacuation was refused on the grounds that in Nova Bila, in another hospital, Croat wounded were not being allowed to be evacuated by the Muslims. We were told that once the Nova Bila wounded had been evacuated, then the Muslim wounded from the east bank could be evacuated. We achieved the evacuation of the wounded from Nova Bila and the evacuation of the wounded from the hospital on the east bank of the river in Mostar was also partially successful. There was clear linkage between the two, but again at this time this was not an unusual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A linkage between two different parts of Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Right, a linkage between what was happening in Mostar and what was happening in Central Bosnia around the area of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the signed summary become Exhibit 2815, please. Two exhibits, both distributed to Defence and also to the Chamber. But one needs to be replaced, because a missing page has now been inserted. So first 1097.1, which is the replacement document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just register an objection to these documents Your Honour, in principle. They have not been delivered to us by the January the 20th deadline that this Court imposed, and I have not seen the third page to which counsel refers, and so we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the Defence have the new copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here they are. Sorry. I can now turn to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I can turn to Exhibit 1097.1, you're not named on this document, but this comes from your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It comes from Mr. Viktor Andreev, who is the head of civil affairs. I'm sorry, it comes from Albert Benabou, who was the civil affairs representative in Mostar, to Viktor Andreev. I am, in fact, named on the one that I'm looking at, Brigadier Hayes, chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the only passage I want you to deal with on this particular document is at the first substantive page after the cover sheet, Mr. Boban's declared positions, where it reads that: "The Vance-Owen Plan is subject to modifications, and those changes must be acceptable to the Croats. "Relations with Mr. Izetbegovic. Izetbegovic must give up the idea of a Muslim state. In the field, there is another reality. "I will never agree to the establishment of a Muslim state," emphasised Mr. Boban. "Fikret Abdic, a Muslim member of the presidency, is considered, according to Mr. Boban's advisors, capable of naming someone who will replace Izetbegovic." And then over the page: "Alija Izetbegovic is my enemy. His declarations in Ankara, Madrid, Paris, and London are against the peace process," specified Mr. Boban. Does that match the sentiments being expressed more generally at the time on your experience?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: It does. I should perhaps point out that I was looking just now at the wrong document. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: My name does not appear on this particular document, but it did go to the headquarters, and I would have seen it. Yes, it does. And as regards the relations with the UNPROFOR paragraph, it would be incorrect to say that, as is stated there, the Croats were the only ones to accept the presence of UNPROFOR. The Muslims had -- or the Bosnians had UNPROFOR stationed. Visoko was an area within their control, and of course Sarajevo itself was an area within their control, so we were stationed on territory which they controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second document I want you to look at is provided necessarily in its complete form, 1145.3, but I want it for one sentence of one of its attachments. But it has to come to you in its complete form. The document, dated the 18th of July, does have your name on it, and if we go in four pages, we come to a very poorly-photocopied, just-readable document from Pogarcic. Have you found that document?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the middle of this letter, which is itself in English, do we see a reference to the milk or the milk convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes, powdered milk for the children of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we see here that the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, it must be Mr. Boban, has instructed all HVO commanders that upon something -- and it goes on. So here is reflected, in this letter, an instruction from the president, Boban, down to the HVO commanders at a local level. Would that be something that you might expect or not expect?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: One would normally expect such direction to go to the commander-in-chief and then be passed on down the military chain of command to the commanders in the field. It's slightly unusual for it to be passed direct, in this manner, to the commanders at a lower level. It perhaps indicates that the commander-in-chief did not exercise complete authority in the manner which one would expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, indeed, in the manner which you didn't find in Petkovic when he tried to exercise authority in relation to the Convoy of Joy?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Brigadier, good afternoon. My name is Stephen Sayers. Together with my colleague, Mr. Naumovski, we represent Mr. Kordic. I understand that you have to be out of here by 4.00 today, and we will make sure that that happens. The first question: With respect to Exhibit Z1145.3 about which you've just spoken, have you ever spoken to Mr. Pogarcic about this document or about the document that is contained in this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever spoken to Mr. Pogarcic at all?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did such orders ever go out, as apparently Mr. Pogarcic relates in his 16th of July 1993 letter?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I can only say if he instructed it. I surmised he did. I could not state categorically that I knew such orders had been passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It remains in the realm of surmise?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever spoken directly to Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. You met with the investigators who worked for the Prosecution and gave them a statement over a three-day period in November of 1996; correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in that statement you referred to a diary. Did you maintain this diary contemporaneously?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the diary in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No, I haven't, because it is in storage in the United Kingdom. I am actually posted in Africa at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, before you took up your position in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you did not receive any specific training, did you?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You just took a media course at the senior staff college, I believe?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct. But I have had a considerable amount of training before that, having completed both the army staff college, the higher commanding staff course, and something called the Royal College of Defence studies, which is a year long course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Brigadier. Please forgive the halting delivery, but since we speak virtually the same language, the interpreters often are challenged, and we can create some serious problems if we overlap. So I'd appreciate it if you'd just have a small delay after each of my questions, and I'll try to do the same, after --

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I apologise. I should have learnt, after six and a half months in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that before you went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, you knew very little about the country or, indeed, about the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And I believe, sir, that you received some briefings from the Ministry of Defence before you took up your duties regarding the British military perspective on Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes. They were in the form really of documentation that I was required to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But it would be accurate, wouldn't it, to say that you actually received no formal briefing from any United Nations organisation in connection with the duties that you assumed as the second in command of UNPROFOR in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That would be correct, but I was not second in command. I was the chief of staff. There was a commander, there was a deputy commander, and then there was the chief of staff. The chief of staff's responsibility is to run the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So you were number three in the chain of command, if you like? Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And without dwelling on that, I take it your immediate predecessor was Brigadier Cordy-Simpson?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, I believe that you made a short reconnaissance visit to Bosnia-Herzegovina just for informational purposes in mid-March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And took up your position of chief of staff to the United Nations command or of the United Nations command on April the 6th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I think I arrived in Kiseljak on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And just so that we all understand your tour of duty, I believe that you handed over to your successor --

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Brigadier Ramsey.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- Brigadier Ramsey, on the 13th of October?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: 13th or 14th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you dealt primarily with military matters, I take it, sir, and you had in your office, or within your headquarters, a civil affairs office that was headed by a career diplomat, Mr. Andreev; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What you tried to do was to complement each other's functions, depending upon whether the particular issue at hand was military or civil?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: We were always talking to each other to make certain that whatever we were doing was -- there was a synergy between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And I believe -- just two or three days after your arrival, you had the opportunity to meet with President Izetbegovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And discuss three things, I believe: Necessary repairs to the sanitary system in Sarajevo; unauthorised crossings into Sarajevo airport, in violation of agreements relating to the airport; and thirdly, your request to President Izetbegovic to allow ethnic Bosnian Serb residents residing in the city of Tuzla to be able to leave and travel to a Serbian enclave, Zvornik, if they wished to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And despite, ostensibly, agreement on all three issues, you noticed very little progress on any of these issues throughout your six month tour in Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, when you come to a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This would be a convenient moment, Your Honour. Just for the Trial Chamber's information, in the interests of expediency, I've prepared a binder of exhibits that I intend to use with Brigadier Hayes. And for everybody's easy reference, I've actually highlighted the points which I want to refer to, so we don't have to flip through papers. And I'd like to distribute those just at the beginning of the session this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Brigadier, would you be back, please, at ten past 2.00, when we will continue your evidence. I must warn you not to speak to anybody about your evidence, until it's over, and don't let anybody speak to you, please. Thank you. Ten past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.40 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon, Brigadier Hayes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Before we broke for lunch, I was just about to turn to the question of the Vance-Owen Plan, about which you made some comments in the statement that's been identified as your evidence today, and I believe that you said, sir, on page 3 of your statement, that on April the 15th, 1993, which was the day before the fighting broke out in the Lasva Valley, your headquarters started work on the military aspects of the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct. We were doing contingency planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if you could just tell us and the Trial Chamber exactly what it was that you were doing in connection with preparing for the military aspects of the implementation of this plan, sir.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: The plan involved certain -- well, the division of the country, and there was some areas of mixed population which were going to different ethnic groups. And it was in those areas that we believed there would be a requirement for a U.N. presence to ensure that there was no violence. That's what we were looking at, and we were assessing the strength that we had against the requirement that might come up if the Vance-Owen Plan was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was it your view, sir, as a high-ranking officer in UNPROFOR, that the Vance-Owen Plan actually called for the ethnic division of Bosnia-Herzegovina and for those divisions to be essentially homogeneous areas; ethnically, that is?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I don't think so. As I remember, there were areas which were still mixed which were to be passed or were to fall under the jurisdiction of either Serbs or Croats or Bosnian. I had no perception of there being what might amount to an ethnic division of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you did not pay a great deal of attention to the political details of the Vance-Owen Plan and the way in which political power was to be distributed and shared in each of the provinces?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In that case, there's not a lot of sense in taking up too much time on this subject, other than to say the following thing, sir. Your primary focus at this time, in the middle of April of 1993, and very understandably, was upon the terrible situation that was occurring in Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That is correct. That was the focus of the United Nations Security Council at the time, and the resolutions that they were passing obviously required work from us for them to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And on April the 16th, when the fighting in the Lasva Valley broke out, your attention was consumed, if you like, with negotiations between Mr. Radavan Karadzic, on the one hand, and Ratko Mladic on the other and -- well, actually between those two; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Well, they weren't negotiating between themselves, no. My attention was focused on discussions at Sarajevo Airport between General Halilovic of the Bosnian army and General Mladic to get a ceasefire around the Srebrenica area, as was called for in United Nations Security Council Resolution 819, I think it was. And subsequently to that and once that ceasefire had been agreed, I was directed by General Volgren and General Morillon to work out the details of it to ensure that humanitarian aid was allowed through to Srebrenica, and a U.N. presence was established there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So there were active negotiations under way is what you're saying, I believe, between General Halilovic, on the one hand, the commander of the ABiH, and General Mladic, the commander of the BSA. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That was the high-level negotiation. Later on, both those commanders-in-chief delegated responsibilities for negotiations to -- General Mladic delegated it to General Gvero, and General Halilovic delegated it to Mr. Siber, Colonel Siber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One matter of detail concerning the Vance-Owen Plan, and then I'll move on to another subject. It's true, is it not, as far as you understand it, that Mr. Karadzic signed the plan on May the 2nd on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs, but it was subject to ratification by the Bosnian Serb assembly or parliament in Pale?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe, sir, that the plan was rejected by that body on May the 6th of 1993.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, but it was rejected by them, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to the fighting that occurred in April, sir, and the negotiations that led to a ceasefire. We know that fighting broke out on April the 16th, and we also know that a ceasefire agreement was negotiated at high level about four days later between General Morillon, Ambassador Jean-Pierre Thebault, Generals Halilovic and Petkovic, and also Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart from BritBat was there, and this ceasefire agreement was negotiated in Zenica. Do you know anything about that ceasefire agreement?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't. I was not involved in those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You were asked some questions during your brief direct examination here today concerning the chain of command and the way in which orders filtered down from the supreme commander of the HVO, who was Mate Boban, to subordinate military commanders. Let me ask you -- let me ask to have distributed the booklet of exhibits that I have put together and, for the Court's information, these have already been distributed both to the Prosecution and to the co-defendant and to the interpreters, Your Honour. I wonder if we could have this marked as a collective exhibit. It has separate tab numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document marked D201/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Brigadier, just for your information, this is an assembly of ten exhibits in total, and I have highlighted the portions which I want to draw your attention to. If you would just turn to Tab 1 on pages 3 and 4 of that tab. This tab is a milinfosum number 170 from the 1st Battalion of the Cheshire Regiment, dated April 18, 1993. And attached to this milinfosum is an agreement reached between President Izetbegovic and Mate Boban for a ceasefire on April the 18th, 1993. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I wonder if I could just ask the usher to place two previously marked exhibits on the ELMO, and this subject need not detain us for very long, sir. The first document, sir, has already been marked D84/1, and it is a copy of an order signed on the same day as the ceasefire agreement negotiated at the very highest level, signed by Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, and carrying into force the four points that were agreed upon by President Izetbegovic and President Boban. Now, speaking from your perspective as a military man, this is the way that you would normally expect the chain of command to work; the supreme commander passes an order down, and then the commander in chief of the armed forces distributes the order to his subordinate operative zones; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And if you would look at the second document, Brigadier, previously marked Exhibit Z715. This is an order entered the same day, or issued the same day by Colonel Blaskic, the commander of the Central Bosnia operative zone, to the brigades and forces under his command, and carrying into force the order previously issued by Brigadier Petkovic, his commanding officer, and by President Boban. Once again, sir, would you agree that that's the way that you would expect the chain of command to work?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That completes the questions I have for that. The next question, Brigadier, concerns the mixed military working group about which you testified today. Would it be fair to characterise the fixed military working group as the only extant form, on a formal basis, that existed for an ongoing dialogue between the three warring factions in Bosnia-Herzegovina: The Bosnian Croats, the Bosnian Muslims, and the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes. But there were mixed military working groups at all levels. The one that I used to attend was the one at the highest levels, between the commanders in chief, and if they delegated to their immediate subordinates, then I would chair those negotiations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, sir, for the Muslim contingent, if I may characterise them that way, General Halilovic initially was the highest -- was initially the commander in chief of the ABiH, to be replaced in the middle of June, I believe, or at the beginning of June, June the 8th to be precise, by General Rasim Delic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I believe General Halilovic was replaced earlier than that, because it was General Delic who came to Kiseljak as commander in chief to negotiate with General Petkovic, when General Petkovic refused to speak to Siber, and that was at the beginning of --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, you've already said that was May the 8th.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. But you would agree that General Halilovic was replaced at some point in May by General Rasim Delic, as the commander in chief?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. And occasionally their deputy, Colonel Siber, would negotiate in the mixed military working group, if his immediate commanding officer was not available; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Either Colonel Siber or Colonel Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: One of those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And for the Croats it was always General Petkovic who was negotiating while you were present with the mixed military working group, or his subordinate, Colonel Lucic, from Mostar. Is that right, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That is correct.
