Though on many occasions -- well, several occasions in Sarajevo, when we were having meetings, it was the commander of the HVO brigade in Sarajevo, whose name I cannot remember at the moment. But he represented the Croats, and Colonel Lucic was always on hand with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And for the Bosnian Serbs it was General Ratko Mladic, who was the principal negotiator, or his deputy, General Gvero; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct. I did not negotiate in Sarajevo Airport with anyone other than General Gvero, though, on the ground I made several or had several negotiations with General Milanovic, the Serbian chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, it's true, is it not, that Mr. Kordic never attended a single one of the mixed military working group meetings that you attended?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No one contended that his attendance was essential, did they?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Or even necessary, important or helpful, for that matter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In fact, it would be fair to say that his name did not crop up, as far as you can remember, during the mixed military working group meetings over which -- at which you were present; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say, sir, at page 5 of your statement, that at some point following the concerns or your involvement with the Srebrenica matters, you turned your attention to the fighting in Central Bosnia, and that you received a briefing from Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart on the 26th of April. You said that on page 5 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Basically, the subjects that you were discussing, and the briefing that you were receiving from your subordinate, was the question of how UNPROFOR could react to dampen down the fighting that was going on in that area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And you both agreed that this was difficult to do, because UNPROFOR had no mandate to become involved in the fighting, one way or the other; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct. But by continuing to operate framework operations, as we called them, and establishing an U.N. presence in the area, it was possible to deter attacks on civilians and also, obviously, it helped to secure the area for the delivery of humanitarian aid. But principally the presence helped to deter attacks on civilians. But you could not be everywhere at the same time, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree that the principal mission of BritBat, anyway, was to facilitate UNHCR aid convoys, the delivery of humanitarian aid to those people that needed it?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That was the mandate as stated, but the mandate was always being stretched.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were briefed, that the military commander in the Vitez-Busovaca pocket was in fact Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, the commander of the Central Bosnia operative zone, under General Milivoj Petkovic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I can remember Blaskic's name coming up. I am sure that I knew he was a commander in the region, but I honestly can't remember the exact detail of what I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Perfectly understandable, sir. It was a long time ago. Now, to the best of your recollection, the name Dario Kordic did not arise during your briefing by Lieutenant-Colonel Stewart, did it?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Not to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you gave some testimony, sir, surrounding a joint ceasefire agreement covering all of Bosnia that was negotiated on May the 8th of 1993, between Generals Halilovic and Mladic. And I believe that a joint statement was prepared and signed by the two Generals and issued -- sort of announced in front of TV cameras. Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And this agreement announced the arrival of a ceasefire for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I take it?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct. Between the Serbs and the Muslims. And it was -- it was a bit of a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, frankly, it didn't come to pass, did it? The Muslims and the Serbs did not cease fighting from May the 8th onwards?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No ceasefire lasted a great length of time, but that was one of the earliest ceasefires, and there was certainly a great deal of hope attached to it, an expectation that for once we might succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Brigadier, no criticism is intended by this comment, but on page 8 of your statement you said that on June the 8th Halilovic was removed from his seat as commander in chief of the Bosnian army and was replaced by General Delic. You may have had a clearer recollection three years ago than you do -- well, three-and-a-half years ago than you do today. Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I remember that General Halilovic had been attending the negotiations. There was a dispute between himself and President Izetbegovic about his attendance at a meeting in Sarajevo. He refused to attend the meeting. He was ordered to attend the meeting. He had to get there in very quick time. He was not able to take the Mount Igman route and pass through the tunnel under the airport. We offered to take him, under UNPROFOR escort. He was an extremely frightened man, but he was ordered to attend by President Izetbegovic, and he came with us. And I believe that is when we negotiated the 8th of May ceasefire. After that, General Halilovic was no longer on the scene, and the next time that we had a negotiation at commander in chief level, it was General Delic who came along. And my understanding was that General Halilovic had handed over command or, perhaps, been removed from command of the Bosnian army, and General Delic had taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, sir. It's the timing of the removal that is of interest to the Defence. And you did say that it was around June the 8th of 1993. Let me just suggest to you that one day after that, actually, on that day, June the 8th, a major offensive was launched by the ABiH in the area of Travnik, and then one day later another major offensive was launched against the HVO by the ABiH in the area of Kakanj. Does that sound consistent with your recollection of the course of the fighting, sir?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I remember that there were Bosnian offensives taking place and the fighting there certainly did flare up at about that time. I can remember there being attacks in Travnik. I can remember there being attacks in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your statement, on page 8 you refer to a meeting of the Joint Operations Centre in Vitez on June the 6th of 1993. Is it your understanding that this was a joint forum established pursuant to the ceasefire agreement negotiated in April, earlier in the year, for Muslims and Croats to list their grievances and to resolve those grievances without fighting?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: On the 6th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Just to --

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: If you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. You just said, on page 8 of your statement: "On the 6th of June --" and I appreciate dates are difficult to remember so many years afterwards, but you said in your statement: "On the 6th of June, I attended a Joint Operation Centre meeting at Vitez. The meeting, attended by the Muslims and the Croats, was used to list violations of the ceasefire or problems that they were having with the other side." Maybe you have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but at this stage I have no recollection of that. I do remember, though, that meetings that occurred at lower levels were quite often used as a forum in which to put forward grievances. The bones of contention were normally the recovery of bodies or the evacuation and exchange of wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask you, sir, were you aware that General Enver Hadzihasanovic, the commander of the 3rd Corps, had, for several weeks prior to the launching of the Travnik offensive and the Kakanj offensive, been refusing to meet with his counterpart, Colonel Blaskic, the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, to negotiate an amicable resolution of differences without open warfare?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I do have recollections of there being difficulty in being able to establish meetings at that level, yes. The exact details of it, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I could ask you to turn to Tab 2, sir, of the documents. We'll go through these fairly quickly. It's the last page that I'm interested in. There, BritBat's intelligence officer makes the observation that: "Our CO's continued attempts to talk constructively with command at 3rd Corps have fallen on deaf ears, and the command appears to be sidestepping the issue." This is a milinfosum from the 1st Battalion of the Prince of Wales Own, number 43, dated the May the 21st, 1993. Does that refresh your recollection a little bit about the problems that were occurring in trying to establish a constructive dialogue between the ABiH commander and the HVO commander?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I can recall at the time that the ABiH had the upper hand, and that having the upper hand, they were reluctant to enter negotiations which would have required a cessation of hostilities. They kept going with their offensives. And my recollection of it is that the HVO were getting quite desperate because they were taking a bit of a beating from the BiH, and that whilst they were very keen to have the negotiations and to stop, the BiH, having the upper hand, were not happy to let them off the ropes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And we can travel through the next few exhibits very quickly, sir. At Tab 3 is a milinfosum from the very next day, number 23, dated May the 22nd, 1993, and the observation is made by BritBat that: "Blaskic has been keen to attend meetings that the commander of the 1PWO PWO," Lieutenant-Colonel Duncan at that time, "had been trying to arrange." And then the milinfosum goes on to say: "But Hadzihasanovic has stated that while he is personally happy to attend, he must first consult with Halilovic, the comment being that it would appear that the commander of the 3rd Corps is prevaricating for some reason, as it is hard to believe that he is unable to contact his next higher command." Were you informed by Lieutenant-Colonel Duncan that these difficulties in establishing a constructive dialogue were occurring?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I was well aware that within the BiH, the requirement to pass orders down the line was -- the reason that orders were not passed down the line or appeared to be ignored at levels was always put down to the lack of communication that the BiH had, and that from their headquarters in Sarajevo, it was not always possible for them to reach their commanders on the ground. Personally, I found that hard to believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Could you just turn to Tab 4. This is another milinfosum four days later, as June is approaching, milinfosum 27, where it's noted that it has been Hadzihasanovic who has proved to be unwilling to attend the meetings that the commanding officer of BritBat was trying to put together. I take it that you received copies of these milinfosums, or extracts of them, on a fairly regular basis.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: All these milinfosums would have been passed into the milinfo or the G2 cell at the headquarters. They would have been consolidated, and a summary of these milinfo summaries themselves would have been passed around the headquarters. I would not have seen each one of these individually unless there was something of particular significance or particular importance in them. So I would have known about it, and it would probably have been presented, in the daily morning briefing that we had, in the summary of the milinfo that was given out at those meetings. I was aware of the difficulty, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Brigadier. If I could ask you to turn to the next milinfosum, number 5 -- Tab 5, rather, milinfosum 37, dated June the 5th, 1993. Before we cover what's on page 2, would you agree that the offensive that was launched in Travnik and Kakanj was an offensive that would have required considerable advanced logistical preparation and involved many thousands of troops?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I don't think necessarily it would have involved considerable logistic preparation. Very briefly, the situation, in a simplistic way, was that the Serbs and, to a lesser extent, the Croat military had heavy weapons and firepower, artillery, tanks. The Muslim strength or the Bosnian strength was in infantry. And in areas where firepower could predominate on the -- could dominate the battlefield, then Serbs and Croats always had the upper hand. In areas where infantry could dominate the battlefield, then the Muslims or the Bosnians would have the upper hand. Consequently, urban areas were the favoured area for the Bosnians to operate in, and wooded areas. It doesn't take a great deal of logistic preparation to get an infantry offensive going. You've got to get the men there, but there are not a tremendous amount of supplies. So from a sort of professional military point of view, logistic preparations would not have been very lengthy for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And in your professional military opinion, Brigadier, wouldn't you agree that the Lasva Valley area was a pretty much ideal battleground for an infantry battle, if you like, with large amounts of wooded, hilly areas overlooking the Lasva Valley, if you like?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes, there was certainly plenty of opportunity for infantry to dominate areas of the battlefield, particularly the urban areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, Brigadier, thank you. Let's just move on to this milinfosum number 37 in Tab 5, the exhibit at which you're looking. Apparently Lieutenant-Colonel Duncan met General Hadzihasanovic, who adopted an extremely hard-line attitude throughout, and left after only 25 minutes to attend another meeting. Apparently, he began the meeting with the assertion that fighting would soon begin in Kakanj, and then goes on to explain why, and then makes the observation that negotiation with the HVO was not an option. Then he also makes the observation that: "Hadzihasanovic and Suvalic," who I think should be "Dugalic", but I stand to be corrected on that, "were disparaging of the international political attempts to resolve the situation in Bosnia, and that the General stated, when informed of impending troop increases, that he had little faith in diplomacy and the political process." And then the observation is made, sir, that the BiH were no longer prepared to restrain themselves and were likely to take the military initiative in the Lasva Valley, where they enjoy a tactical advantage over the HVO, which I think is broadly consistent with what you have just said. And there's nothing surprising in these comments to you, as you read them seven years later, is there?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No. No surprise at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you would turn to the next milinfosum, sir, June the 6th, which is two days before the BiH offensive started. The last page contains the comment that: "The prospects for the ceasefire holding in Travnik look remote, with both sides demonstrating little faith in the motives of the other." And then the observation is made that: "3rd Corps, judging by the attitude of its commander, seems poised for further military action, having clearly rejected the concept of negotiation." And then the observation is made that: "The restraining influence at present may well be the progress north of the large convoy destined for Tuzla." At the time that you were discussing with General Petkovic some arrangements regarding this Tuzla convoy, sir, were you aware that a large offensive had been launched in the Travnik region, around Travnik and Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes. We knew that there was an offensive and there was fighting there, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The next tab, sir, continues the story, and on the third page -- it's actually marked with a "5" at the bottom. 00273938 is the number. It says that: "1PWO," presumably Lieutenant-Colonel Duncan, "met Enver Hadzihasanovic last week. He remarked that Kakanj would be the next town to experience fighting. Similarly, two independent visitors to 3rd Corps HQ today were told that fighting was taking place in the town." And that's the 9th of June, sir.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: What page are we looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's page -- it's stamped on the bottom "00273938". Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes. It's paragraph 17, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And if you could just turn to the last page, sir, this milinfosum is dated two days before the Convoy of Joy incident, about which you testified and which we'll cover in just a minute, but the observation is made that: "It would appear that Enver Hadzihasanovic and 3rd Corps are orchestrating a carefully-planned and phased attack against the HVO in the areas of Travnik and the western Lasva Valley. In this context, Hadzihasanovic's constant refusals to meet Blaskic and his failure to attend negotiations concerning the situation in Travnik during that phase of the current fighting perhaps receive explanation." Other observations are made on that page, and we can all read them. There's no point in belabouring the issue. But there is no question, sir, that the BiH were militarily dominant in the Lasva Valley and that they were actually prosecuting their advantage at the beginning of June of 1993. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now let's turn to the Convoy of Joy. On June the 11th, the ABiH offensive had been going on for three days. Were you aware that large numbers of refugees -- it's been estimated by the European Community Monitoring Mission that there were as many as 20.000 Bosnian Croat refugees as a result of that fighting -- were you aware that large numbers of refugees had flooded into the Lasva Valley just shortly before the Convoy of Joy arrived?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Again, I cannot remember exact details, but I would not be the least bit surprised if refugees had been -- well, people had been displaced by the fighting and would be moving to areas that they considered to be areas of safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And these were, just so the record is clear, because I think there's been an omission, these were Bosnian Croat refugees, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: They would be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, that it would really be suicidal to route a convoy, organised by Muslims to provide aid to the beleaguered and besieged town of Tuzla, to route that convoy straight through the middle of an active war zone?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I don't think it's suicidal. Convoys were going through the whole time, because UNHCR convoys were going through, NGO convoys were going through. So suicidal, I think, is a bit of a strong term.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I agree with you, but this was not an UNHCR convoy, was it?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No, nor were some of the NGO convoys that went through. This was not an isolated convoy that didn't have UNPROFOR protection. There were other convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But it was a private convoy, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: It was organised by the Muslims in Tuzla. Yes, it was, if you like, a commercially organised convoy, and a large one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And so this convoy organised by the Muslims was routed right up through the main supply route that led to Novi Travnik, intended to take a right turn on the main Travnik to Vitez road, go right through Vitez to Zenica, on its way north, in the middle of a very large ABiH offensive?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact route that it was due to take, but it was certainly coming up into the Vitez pocket, traversing through the Vitez pocket and then north to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would agree, sir, would you not, that a purely private convoy was not within the mandate of BritBat to protect?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I've already said that it wasn't an UNHCR sponsored convoy, therefore, as I said to General Petkovic, the United Nations could not escort it. What we did do, because we anticipated that there could be difficulty, that's why we were asking General Petkovic to ensure its safe passage, the British Battalion did have its Warrior armoured vehicles out on positions throughout the route, almost to picket it, if you understand that sort of old fashioned expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. One final question on this subject, on this particular aspect of the subject. In this picket duty, as you phrased it, British soldiers opened fire on the HVO and actually killed three --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've had evidence about this. There is little point in going over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President, but only insofar as this witness provides an identification of the number of HVO soldiers that were killed. There is some fuzziness in the evidence in that, and I believe the Brigadier puts it at three.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I honestly -- again, I can't remember. The number does seem to strike a chord, but the British certainly only opened fire after the convoy had been fired on itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: And that would be within the mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: A stretched mandate, admittedly, but protecting civilian life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move onto your involvement in the events of June the 11th. Were you aware that there had been a serious incident the night before you arrived in the area in which eight small children had been killed when an artillery shell exploded in a playground in which they were killing?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, do I understand it to be the case that you had not spoken to Mr. Kordic ever, prior to June the 11th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you've never spoken to him after that date, I take it?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No. I spoke to him twice, when I was down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Twice on one day. Right. But from June the 12th to this very day, you've never spoken to him again, right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I have not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So you only met him on two occasions on one day, in your entire six-month tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know what his position was?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I understood, from talking to the people on the ground, not exactly what his position was, but that he did have the authority within the pocket to ensure that the convoy would be going through, and could go through safely. And from what I had learnt from General Petkovic, as I have already said, his authority appeared to be limited in that area. And I was told, when I asked the question, that the man who did have the authority, who could guarantee the safety of the convoy, was Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let's take that one at a time. You had dealt with General Petkovic fairly regularly before this incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And he was a military man, a professional military man who spoke your language; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. What did he tell you about Mr. Kordic's authority in the Vitez-Busovaca pocket, if anything?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I never asked him, and it was never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Well, who did you speak to, to determine exactly what Mr. Kordic's position was, and what the parameters of his powers were, if any?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I believe that we -- when I was briefed in BritBat, his name may have come up, but I cannot guarantee that. All I can tell you is that when I went out on the ground, and the looting was happening, and the vehicles were being hijacked, that the people on the ground, when I asked with Ambassador Thebault, how we could stop this, who had the authority, I was directed to go to Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And who directed you to go to Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: The individuals who were on the ground. They would have been HVO soldiers, officers probably. I cannot remember exactly. But it was no surprise to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were they or weren't they officers or soldiers, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I cannot remember at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I take it, that you didn't make any notes as to whom you spoke?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No, not -- if it's not done in the statement, as exactly to whom I spoke on the ground, no. But Ambassador Thebault was there and it seemed to be no surprise to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether these people were members of the home guard, or members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: They were members of the HVO, as far as I could ascertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I had no doubt in my own mind that I was talking to people on the ground who, having hijacked vehicles -- that there was a chain of command there. The people on the ground were not prepared to stop it. And when I asked them, they passed me up the line metaphorically to Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. It wouldn't be particularly surprising, in an area thronged by refugees, sir, for the political figure to be pointed to, in a time of turmoil such as this. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You wouldn't?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't agree because it wasn't a political matter. It was a straightforward matter of indiscipline by soldiers on the ground; soldiers and policemen, for that matter, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Kordic give any orders to military people, sir?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Because when I spoke to him, he assured me he was doing his best, and that he would gather the convoy together; that there were no -- no, I could not -- I could not swear that there were people there to whom he could have passed the order, when I spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it's true that you didn't engage him in any dialogue at all, as to what his military power was, if any, did you?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No, I had no reason to engage him in any military dialogue, as you put it. I was merely there with Ambassador Thebault, because he was the person I was directed to, by people on the ground, involved in the looting, involved in the hijacking of the vehicles, clearly acting in an undisciplined way. I was directed to him as the person who could put a stop to that and who could gather together the remnants of the convoy and get them under the protection of the British Battalion in the quarry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Was there anybody else at this meeting, other than you and Ambassador Thebault? Lieutenant-Colonel Duncan, for example?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No, Colonel Duncan was not there. He was out on the ground, as far as I can recall, commanding his battalion and getting the vehicles -- getting the lorries from the convoy that were scattered in the pocket, shepherded as far as he could into the quarry. There were some other people there. I cannot remember who they were. I would surmise that Anto Valenta was there, because subsequently he led us to the quarry. But I could not again swear that he was present during these discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Nothing wrong with that. You just can't remember. It was a long time ago. As far as you remember, it was Ambassador Thebault, you, Mr. Kordic and maybe some others?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: And I suspect -- or I believe, if it was not Anto Valenta who was there, he certainly came to the area because he was the one who undertook to take leaders to the quarry. We had a certain amount of difficulty in finding where Mr. Kordic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No. He was a political figure, I believe, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is not, sir, is there, a single reference in your statement of three years ago, given to the Prosecution's investigators, to the effect that you made an inquiry as to who you should see, and you were directed, by persons unknown, to go and see Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: If there isn't, then it should be in there, because I can remember full well asking on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask you, see if I can jog your memory on this. Had you been briefed that Mr. Kordic was the vice-president of the presidency of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I understood that he had links with Mr. Boban, but at what stage that information came to me, I honestly again don't know. At this stage of the time that I was in Bosnia, what was happening in Central Bosnia was very much new territory to me. I had been entirely focused on Srebrenica, on the problems between Muslims and Serbs. What was happening in the Lasva Valley was very largely left to the British Battalion, as a very effective organisation, which again almost had its own chain of command down to the British Brigadier, who was the senior British officer on the case. And indeed, they were more likely to pass information and answer to them than they were to the United Nations. So this was new. I do know that I was told at some stage that Dario Kordic had links to Mr. Boban. I understood at some stage that -- I understood them to be Mr. Boban's deputy and a political military figure, but at what stage I was told that, I'm afraid I could not tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall whether you were told that he was one of the vice-presidents of the Croat political party or the principal Croat political party, the HDZ-BiH?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I mean, when you say he was a vice-president, it does strike a chord in my mind, but again, at what time? I wouldn't -- I honestly could not say. I mean, when I -- I can only go back to saying, in regard to all of this, that I had not seen Dario Kordic before, I had not had dealings with Colonel Blaskic. Indeed, it wasn't until right near the end of my time that I met Colonel Blaskic. When I went into the pocket, it was to assess the situation, give direction to the British Battalion, who were under pressure, who had stretched the mandate, in the action trying to protect the convoy. When I saw the looting happening on the ground, I enquired as to who had the authority to stop this, because nobody on the ground appeared either to have the authority or the inclination to stop it. And I was directed to Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever subsequently discuss this incident, the Convoy of Joy incident with General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No, I don't think I saw General Petkovic. I don't know when I next saw him. General Petkovic, at some stage, almost vanished from the scene. I have a feeling that shortly after this time we didn't actually see him again. I cannot say that I spoke to General Petkovic about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've described the attitude that you saw in Mr. Valenta, in the HVO troops regarding this convoy, as one of indifference. You can certainly understand why the attitude would be one of indifference, given the offensive that was taking place against the HVO simultaneously, can't you?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes. You can understand it in that context. But indifference to the convoy does not give you any reason or any right to kill drivers, to hijack vehicles, to loot vehicles. Indifference is not a strong enough reason to let actions like that continue under your very nose, if you are a military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: And the convoy was civilian. There were no military in the convoy. They were civilian. And the drivers were pulled out of the cab, as I understand it, and they were shot. Indeed, I think some were killed in other rather more unpleasant ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You met Mr. Kordic the second time on June the 11th, later in the evening, I believe, and he told you that he was doing his best to try to repacket or repackage the convoy; right? Would you just turn to Tab 8 of the exhibit, where the observation says that: "The restrictions on the free movement of the Convoy of Mercy would appear to have been lifted in accordance with Dario Kordic's instructions of yesterday. The dispersed vehicles had been repacketed and moved relatively unmolested to the Zenica mountain road where BiH control begins." Just one question, sir.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The highlighted language there. Do you know what Mr. Kordic did or to whom he spoke to try to resolve this situation?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing any vehicles come into the quarry while I was there, other than escorted by the British Battalion. I did not see any vehicles that were brought in by HVO. The only vehicles that I saw in possession of the HVO were ones that were hijacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Brigadier, we are making very good progress. I don't have very much for you. Just one question in connection with paragraph 17 of the statement that you signed relating to the town of Fojnica. You say that despite an agreement signed on the 13th of June 1993, on the 2nd of July, fighting spread to -- fighting which had been north of Kiseljak spread to Fojnica. You were instrumental in discussions that were directed to having the town of Fojnica declared a safe area, or a safe haven?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you met all of the Croat Muslim political, religious, and military leaders, right? And they all agreed to try to cooperate to avoid a conflict and to avoid interethnic tensions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, in fact, the agreement, so signed on June the 13th, supported, I believe, by the local military commanders, made Fojnica a so-called "peace area," is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's right. They wished to see it established as a safe area, in the same way that other areas had been so designated by the U.N. Security Council. That was not possible, and they then opted to make Fojnica an area of medical importance, I think was the phrase that was used, under the Geneva Convention, because there were some hospitals there, and which particularly specialised in rehabilitation of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if you would just turn to Tab 10 in the package, which is an European Community Monitoring Commission background report concerning the condensed history of events in Fojnica, and it's dated October the 6th, 1983. Just by way of background, Brigadier, I believe that on June the 30th, your commanding officer, General Morillon, came down to Fojnica and held up Fojnica to the world as an example of what could be achieved, if the two sides and their leaders genuinely wanted to live in harmony, right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All of the international press was there, so far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: -- was there, certainly. Fatal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then two days later the ABiH attacked Fojnica and basically displaced approximately 6.500 of the Croat population that lived in that town; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I don't know how many people were displaced. Certainly fighting began, and subsequently I learned that it was, or I was told that it was a Bosnian army attack, probably the 7th Muslim Brigade. They were not people who were involved in the town itself or in the agreement. They were forces that came from outside, which was the one thing that both sides in Fojnica feared would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that in your experience in your six month tour, the 7th Muslim Brigade could regularly be expected to be seen whenever there was fighting going on?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: There was so much -- I know what you mean, but when there was fighting going on in Central Bosnia, there was always the talk of the 7th Muslim Brigade being used. It was as much a psychological ploy as anything else. Certainly, they were effective infantry, shock troops, if you like. Quite often, the 7th Muslim Brigade was announced as being on its way, with the psychological -- to give a psychological impact and to actually create fear in people. They certainly could not have been in as many different places as they were alleged to have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. If you would just turn to the second page of Tab 10, sir, right at the bottom. Observations are made by the ECMM to the effect that only 150 Croats were left in town, that before the fighting began, 41 per cent of the population, or 6.600 people were of Croat ethnicity, and that the majority had left for Kiseljak. And that prior to their departure, they had been subjected to discrimination and the other things that this report goes into. Is that consistent with your recollection of the events that occurred in Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I can remember the fighting. The fighting split the population. The town, I believe, fell into the hands of the Bosnians. The Croat front line moved to the east -- the far side of actually a handicapped childs hospital. Whether the Croat population of Fojnica was subject to intimidation or not, I don't know. The two communities did want to live together. I expect, when people are coming from inside, particularly if the word is that it's the 7th Muslim Brigade, the sensible would leave in fear of their lives and would have gone to the nearest perceived safe area, which would have been Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I am now through with the package of exhibits. So you can close that up. I just have a few subjects to touch upon before I close. Would it be fair to say, sir, that following the Convoy of Joy incident, you turned your attention immediately to higher level affairs, if you like, at Sarajevo Airport, and that you presided over discussions between Generals Mladic, Delic, and Petkovic on June the 15th at a mixed military working group meeting?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, but certainly attention switched back to Sarajevo, which at that stage was again becoming the centre of the International Community's interest; and the beginning of the American desire to use aircraft to destroy or contain the Serb artillery was beginning to hit the headlines, and also the whole saga of the siege of Sarajevo was beginning to capture everybody's attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You also --

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's not to say, though, that the fighting in Central Bosnia was not important. There was a lot of fighting going on there. And there were certain things that did focus our attention. One was the plight of the refugees in Kakanj. We ended up with a group of them living with the French battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Those were Bosnian Croat refugees?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me try to conclude this fairly quickly. You talked in your statement about some problems that occurred in Kiseljak in July of 1993, in Visoko, where Mr. Lucic and Ivica Rajic attended a party given by the Canadian Battalion in Visoko, and the base was surrounded, because the Bosnian Muslims wanted to arrest these two gentlemen; correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, your base of operations, unless I am much mistaken, was, in fact, in Kiseljak, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's where the United Nations headquarters was, the headquarters for the United Nations protection force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you never, throughout your six month tour of duty, ever saw Mr. Kordic actually in Kiseljak itself?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No. It was not that easy to move from Vitez to Kiseljak, because anybody would have to go through the territory that was controlled by the Muslims and cross over at least two if not more front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I'm not sure about what the answer was, but I think the answer was that you never, in fact, saw him in Kiseljak. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And as far as you're aware, what political influence he had, if any, you never saw any manifestation of that in Kiseljak or the Kiseljak pocket because it was completely surrounded by that time during your six-month tour of duty as the third in command of UNPROFOR; would that be fair to say as well?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I didn't see him in Kiseljak at all. The only -- or the person we dealt with for most of the time in Kiseljak was Vinko Lucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. But no one ever said that if a problem cropped up, for example, that needed a swift solution, or any kind of a long-term solution, for that matter, that it would be Mr. Kordic that you would have to see?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Not in Kiseljak, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who would that person have been?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: In Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Lucic; is that --

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Colonel Lucic was the UNPROFOR -- the liaison officer, and if there was a problem there, we would have spoken to him. He would have probably spoken to the local commander, Rajic. But to be honest, the position that Vinko Lucic actually held, the degree of authority and power he had was never entirely clear to me. Rather more than he professed, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about the linkages between evacuations of wounded in Eastern Mostar and the hospital at Nova Bila. Isn't it true, sir, that General Hadzihasanovic was a thorn in your side, if you like, and caused you great difficulty by refusing to allow the Nova Bila evacuation?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Certainly the Nova Bila evacuation was blocked, yes, and he, as the commander there, would have had a hand in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, he informed you that if you tried to move the wounded out of Nova Bila, forces under his command would open fire on any BritBat vehicles moving the wounded; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I seem to recollect some threat like that, yes. At the same time, no one was being allowed to be evacuated from East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You said on page 11 of your statement: "In particular, 3rd Corps Commander Hadzihasanovic refused to allow the evacuation from Nova Bila and threatened to fire on any BritBat vehicles moving wounded." Does that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We did eventually achieve the -- that again is an example of the linkage. He refused to allow them to be evacuated because of what was happening in East Mostar. It wasn't just a Serb who linked things. All three sides would link activities in various areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Brigadier, I'm much obliged for your testimony today. Thank you very much. That concludes my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Brigadier. My name is Goran Mikulicic, and together with my colleague, Mr. Kovacic, I'm Defence counsel for the second accused. I am going to put a few questions to you simply to clarify some of the points that you spoke about. Let us go back to the convoy for a few minutes, please. If I understood your testimony correctly, the convoy was stopped in the area of Novi Travnik, and you described that as the Vitez pocket in a broader sense; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct. It was stopped, as I understand it, in the area of the front lines on the edge of what I describe as the Vitez pocket, but it was to the west of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In an effort to work out this situation, you conducted certain meetings, you talked to people. You already explained this to us. Brigadier, were you aware of the fact that in the town, Vitez, the command of the Operative Zone for that area was located and that Colonel Blaskic was the top military person in that area; were you aware of that fact at the time?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I knew that Colonel Blaskic -- I knew Colonel Blaskic by name as the Croat -- a Croat commander, the Croat commander in the area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Although you were aware of that, nevertheless you did not even try to talk to Colonel Blaskic in order to resolve the situation regarding the convoy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct, because when I went out on the ground, it was not to Colonel Blaskic that I was directed by people on the ground to get what was happening to the convoy stopped; it was to Dario Kordic, not to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, there was another high-ranking military officer there, and that was General Petkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No. General Petkovic at that time had left. General Petkovic had been in Kiseljak with us, carrying out some negotiations as I have explained. He contacted Vitez, the HVO in Vitez, about the convoy using the communications of the HVO in their Kiseljak headquarters. This failed to secure the release of the convoy. General Petkovic then had to leave to go to Mostar to carry out some other duties; I believe in relation to the fighting that was going on there. He undertook to go via the Vitez pocket. Indeed, that was probably the only way that he could go. He personally went to the scene where the convoy was being held, attempted to secure its release, but again failed. He then left the scene. General Petkovic was not there when subsequently I went to Vitez. He had left the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. However, you do know that before you came, General Petkovic was in the area where the convoy was stopped; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Brigadier, to the best of your knowledge and according to the chain of command that exists in an army, when a top-ranking military person is in a certain area, does that person then exercise total authority over the entire military in that area?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: When General Petkovic was there, his authority should have been supreme, to use a rather grand phrase. Yes, as the senior commander, his authority would supersede the authority of other commanders on the ground, though I do not know who Colonel Petkovic -- General Petkovic actually met.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Brigadier. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A couple of things, please, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Such convoys as this, how common were they?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: This was, from the size of it and the way that it was organised, unique. But there were other convoys that went through -- from non-governmental organisations that went through unescorted by UNPROFOR, unorganised by UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To reach the Vitez pocket, would this convoy have passed over other territory that was Croat-controlled?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes. It did start from the coast, from Split. It traversed or moved north through Croat-controlled territory. It would have followed, as far as I know, the only route that would have been open to it, which was known as Route Diamond, which went -- it went through the Gornji Vakuf area and so would have gone through Croat-controlled territory predominantly and small areas where the Muslims controlled the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On reaching the Vitez pocket, would it have confronted a checkpoint of some kind?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: There would have been a checkpoint on the road on the front lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which, I suppose, would there have been the option of turning it back and refusing it entry?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: There is always that option. I suspect that physically it would have been quite difficult to turn the convoy around. But, yeah, the option would have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any suggestion that the Croat-controlled checkpoint had said "No"?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: "No" to the passage of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the convoy was blocked. It was not allowed to move forward at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then it was hijacked?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: There were, as I remember it, there were -- they were there for quite some time. The situation got quite heated. There was then some shooting. Some drivers were killed. And at that stage, vehicles were hijacked and the convoy scattered, as it were, rather like a flock of frightened birds. It scattered northwards, and it was almost a case of each driver for himself to try and get through Vitez and on up to Zenica and safe territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How were the other drivers killed who weren't shot?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I understand that they were actually taken -- pulled out of the vehicles and killed by women using pitchforks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You spoke of the distress of the man in charge of the convoy. Were you able to judge whether his expectations of success with this convoy had initially been genuine?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Very genuine. I don't believe he had any suspicion that he would not be allowed to travel through to the north. He might have had a fear that he would be stopped and would have to hand over some of the goods that he was carrying by way of a bribe, if you like, or a levy to get through. But for the vehicles to be hijacked and for people to be killed was totally and utterly shocking and surprising to him, and as I say, he was on the verge of a breakdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any other route to bring food to the civilians in the area to which he was taking this convoy?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No, it was the only route that the convoy could have followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that known generally to everyone at the time?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I'm sure it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked about your knowledge or, more particular, your ignorance of Kordic before this incident. You've told us, and we needn't go into it again, of the judgement you formed of him. But does it follow from what you've told us that you didn't approach this issue with any prejudgement of the man because you knew very little about him?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: That would be correct. I had not met him before. I knew very little of him. I went to the person to whom I was directed, believing that this was the man who could guarantee the safe passage of the convoy or get the vehicles collected back together that had been scattered, but I was not reassured by the meeting with him. I didn't have any faith in his words. When he said that he was doing his best, I regret that I did not believe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked about why you didn't press him, perhaps, for his identified authority, but tell us, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: He was dressed in a camouflaged uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With or without insignia or with anything else around his neck, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And two other things, different topics. Yes, Petkovic. Did Petkovic suggest that you should turn your attention to Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: No. No. General Petkovic went to the area to exercise his own authority. It was never suggested that we should speak to Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other general questions, each very short. You've been asked about the comparative success of the BiH as opposed to the HVO at the time you were in the area, and the use of the word "dominant" was made. But can you give us any comment on the comparative weaponry of the two sides or not?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Yes. As I alluded to in what I was saying, the strength of the Serbs and, indeed, the Croats was that they had greater access to heavy weaponry than did the Muslims. The Bosnian army or the Muslim army was predominantly infantry and would have used small arms and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And finally you've been asked about authority in and communication from Kiseljak. Did you know, one way or another, by what means, if any, people were communicating from Kiseljak to other parts of the Lasva Valley by telephone and/or by means of transport?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: There were telephone lines. I believe that the HVO had its own radio net, and I believe there were radio communications from Kiseljak to Vitez, a normal military communication network.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And any transport communication of which you were aware?

utterances.speaker: GUY DE VERE WINGFIELD HAYES
utterances.text: Not that I was aware of. If somebody -- if a Croat wanted to travel from Kiseljak to Vitez, he would normally ask to travel with us. I mean you could go there, but it was quite dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Brigadier, that concludes your evidence. You are released. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there are one or two administrative matters before we break. The first is something which we want to raise about the international armed conflict. Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice and Mr. Sayers, it seems to me that the essential questions relating to this issue are questions of law and, in some cases, fact, mixed law and fact. The exhibits, in my view, would generally be admissible, the Chamber being left to determine what weight to attach to them. For that reason, I don't think it is necessary to have any prolonged hearing on this. In fact, I think a hearing could be obviated and replaced by written submissions on this question, highlighting the important areas, areas that are important to each party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suppose Mr. Lopez-Terres, who I think has charge of those particular binders at the moment, may be pleased to know that an oral submission would not be required at the moment. We, of course, would be only too pleased to put in a written submission. I don't know whether it's thought that it's appropriate now, before the ending of the Prosecution's case, or if, like all other submissions, it should come simply in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think it can come in due course. That would be in order. Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had anticipated that the international armed conflict documents would be treated pretty much identically with the other documents. I think that with the exception of the objections which we've noted on our charts to illegible documents, documents that aren't signed and so forth, most of those objections -- actually, the illegibility objections, I think, are valid. The other objections pretty much go to weight, as the Trial Chamber has stated in the past, and, frankly, I don't see that a hearing on the issue would be particularly necessary because we would simply be ventilating the same arguments that have already been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad to see we're ad idem on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider whether we should exclude any of the documents. If there are illegible and that sort of documents, that would have to be attended to. But that apart, we'll admit the documents and order submissions, the Prosecution certainly to put in a document explaining what they rely on in the exhibits; Defence, if they wish to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm almost certain that we would wish to respond, and with the Court's permission, we would like to do so in due course, having seen the arguments of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, within two weeks of the close of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sure we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and two weeks for the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That seems fair, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although in light of Judge Robinson's observation about it being a matter for the Chamber to decide, I think the presentation will be a summary and general, rather than laborious and specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I know Mr. Sayers wants to raise something, and I know what it is, but there's also another witness. Now, that witness, Mr. Hamill, has been here since the weekend. I think his time for getting away this afternoon to catch a plane is half past 5.00. He won't actually be very long in chief. His summary, I hope, has already been distributed. But even if it hasn't, his presentation will not take very long. I don't know if there's any way that the Chamber can at least try to accommodate him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I would hope so, if he's been here since the weekend. Is there extensive cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The next witness is an artillery ballistics expert witness. We have not previously been provided with a written report, as I understand, as required by Rule 94 bis, but we're prepared to go ahead with this cross-examination anyway. Just as with the previous witness, in the interests of time, I've prepared a highlighted binder of exhibits that I would distribute, which we should be able to go through fairly quickly. But I doubt that we'll be through in one hour, Your Honour, I really do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be, if the Prosecution are quick, an hour and a quarter will be available. It may be convenient to take the adjournment now and begin a few minutes before 4.00. We'll deal with this question about the statement when we've got time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we regard that as a fairly serious matter, as I'm sure the Court can understand, and we would like to be heard on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We'll adjourn now until five to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might just jump in. It seems to me that in order to utilise the time most efficiently, we could take this statement as read, since it's essentially an expert report, and jump immediately into cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just clarify a few things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Full name, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: John Gerard Brenton Hamill.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see you've done over 25 years in gunnery in Bosnia, elsewhere around the world, and you've also been an instructor. One point of amplification, is calculating the place from which artillery fires a practical skill used by soldiers on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reason being, that if you are being fired at, and you can't see where the guns are firing from, you actually need to work it out?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: You need to work it out in order to return fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that a skill, therefore, in which artillery officers are trained?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And were you so trained?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next point, just to deal with what's contained in your summary, and indeed in your statement, because the Judges don't have the full statement, necessarily. You are concerned here with the shelling of Zenica, but you didn't go and conduct an examination at Zenica until the 6th of April 1997, or thereabout?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you spent how many days conducting your examination?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I spent a full week, at that time, between here and Zenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is a video, which is cued to be played, of Zenica at the time. It's exhibit number -- I'll come to the exhibit number. 2258. I am not going to ask that it all be played, but just a small portion of it, or a portion of it so that we can see what this video amounts to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you find anything you want to comment on. This was a contemporaneous video of Zenica shelling. Apart from showing people who had been killed, does it from time to time shows sites of and even some detail of where the shells landed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Unhappy details. More for the general quality of the film and the sort of detail it was showing. Right. I am going to pause there, because of want of time. Did you see the whole of this film, which is --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- available? Were you able, although you didn't see the film at the time, to compare what that contemporaneous film showed of the scene and of where the shells fell with your own examination conducted in 1997?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to do a comparison. And also, I had photographs taken at the time, which I also used to compare to the ground, as I saw it, with documentary data.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those photographs are 2281, I think you'll find -- I must be incorrect. The three pictures from 2281. Thank you. Two pictures from 2281. Take mine. That won't do. To save time, can you use my photographs, and we'll just use those and we'll make sure we get the right numbers attached to them later. Thank you very much. Just look at these three photographs in sequence and tell us the sort of things of significance that you can see on those photographs. They will be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: This was the scene of the sixth shelling. You can see where the crater has been formed underneath the bus shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Next photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: This was the second shell that fell in Zenica to that day, at 1210 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see on our screen, somewhat indistinctly, marks going out from the central position. Are they of significance in working out the origin of a piece of artillery shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: They certainly are. They are what we use. They are called strikes, and we use the direction of the strikes to fix the direction that the round is coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Using this photograph, explain that general technique, please, to the learned Judges.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: In general terms, although it can't be seen from a photograph, and it's not possible to do crater analysis, per se, from a photograph, the pattern of the shells is very distinctive, particularly when it falls on hard ground like this, asphalt, concrete or whatever. And by laying sticks along, or taking compass bearings along the strikes, particular strikes, which are the widest, you then work out, by having the angle, the direction to the gun in question. So in general terms with this, because the strikes are mainly this way and this way, the round would have come in from that side. But that's very general. It can't be specifically done from a photograph. It must be done on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there a hemispherical distribution of these strikes, or semicircular distribution of the strikes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: More or less semicircular, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness wait for the end of the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- half round plastic compass, as it were, plastic --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Protractor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Protractor. And the flat bit, is that the direction from which the shells come? The other bit. The round bit.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: [No audible answer]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last photograph, please. Just to give a general --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please pause between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are being asked to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Once again, we have a photograph of the 6th shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you please now lay on the overhead projector -- when you went to examine the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are getting the B/C/S on our channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It should be okay now. The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All should be well. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the objection is this. We think it's unbelievable that one day before the close of the Prosecution's case we should be getting brand new exhibits which have never previously been produced to us before, especially exhibits which were apparently prepared in 1997. It's all the more remarkable --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please, Mr. Sayers. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- witness who has not prepared a report that's been provided to us, and this exhibit is now going to be introduced through this expert without a report. We simply haven't been given this before. I think it's too late now. The order that the Court has entered, requiring delivery of all exhibits to us by the 28th of January, is as clear as a bell, and there is just no excuse for late delivery. So we object to it under these circumstances. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I gather that, as a matter of fact, the map is in the Zenica binder. But, in any event, it's referred to in the witness statement. And I am sorry if it didn't go out with the witness statement, as I discovered today. It could have been asked for. It could have been found in the Zenica binder. In any event, the statement, which the Defence have had now for months or a year or so or whatever it is, provides the source information that is being plotted on this plan, and so, of course, it's less than ideal, and I wish that they had had it earlier. It's going to save time rather than do anything else to use the map. The map is the best exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does it say anything new?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. It says what's -- it says what's in the statement, so far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit this document, first of all, because we are told it was -- it had been part of the Zenica binder. In any event, it is merely stating what the evidence says in sketch form. The Defence can, of course, cross-examine upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, will you please explain, rather than me going through questions and answers, the plan and the markings on it dealing with the craters, in the order in which they were formed.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: The first two craters were formed at 1210 by shells falling in this area here [indicates]. The letters "MPI" stand for mean point of impact, which is the spot between the two shells. The second pair fell here [indicates] and here. Again, within a very short period of time, at around 1224. And the final two shells fell here and here, at approximately 1229. And that concluded the shelling on that day. Now, what I can say about them, that for the first and this third pair, as such, there was a distance between them of between 14 and 30 metres. There was a considerably greater distance between the 3rd and the 4th, which were also almost contemporaneous. This has been explained in the report. My reading of it was that there was a slight error on the third round, an error of range or elevation, because the bearing is consistent with the 1st and the 5th rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's, to avoid any confusion of technical language, pick up first the bearing, that is the direction from which the shells had come.
