Did you have two sources of information: One, your observations on the ground of the actual shell craters, where they were left; and two, information coming from ECMM monitors, some of whom we've heard, who conducted their own calculations of bearings at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I initially had a report from the ECMM, a crater analysis. When I examined the craters on the ground, I found no reason to disagree with their analysis, although some -- quite a considerable time had passed. The craters in most cases were still clear enough to get the general direction, not a specific direction in mils, but certainly the general direction within a few degrees left or right of the direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we look at the numbers one and two on the bottom of the three pairs, just remind us again how close were they together?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: They were about -- they were about 14 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the arrow shows the direction from which it is being suggested those two shells came.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct. West.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then the next two up, which are a little further short, they didn't travel quite so far, it would appear. Same general bearing, 4.800. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is quite correct, 4.800 mils.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Their distance apart?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Their distance apart was, if I remember, about 70 metres. However, that is not the significant aspect. What is significant is their deviation from a centre line between them. Both them lay astride the centre line, which is the line drawn on as 4.800 mils; one slightly north by a few metres, and one slightly south by a few metres. They were consistent as regards bearing, but not as regards range.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last pair at the top, how close together?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Thirty metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't yet dealt with, but you must know your source of information as to the order in which these shells fell; was that from ECMM monitors or from some other source?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to witnesses on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One or two or how many?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Numerous. We spent several days in Zenica, and I spoke to considerable numbers of people who had been there during the shelling; those who lived in houses beside where the shells fell, other witnesses who were brought to me by MUP. I must emphasise that I had no direct, personal knowledge of the times myself, and got it from witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there consistency or inconsistency in the accounts that you were given as to the order of the shells?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: There was considerable consistency. And the most consistent fact that I came across was that the shells were described as falling in the three groups of two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they all hit the ground directly, or did any of them land up first somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Four of the rounds impacted on the ground. One of them impacted on the wall of a house in Stari Carcija [phoen], and one of them impacted on a tree just outside the radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the basis that they fell in the order that you've heard, in the three groups of two, what was your conclusion as to the number of pieces of artillery that were firing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I concluded that there were two pieces of artillery in use. Given the fragments that I had -- was given, which purported to be from those shellings, it seemed to me quite clear that it was a D-30 J-gun which fired. This is a hand-loaded weapon, which takes time to fire a second time. Only a certain number of rounds can be fired from it in a minute. So if there were only five seconds between the shells being fired, the logic was that two guns were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What, if anything, is the significance or what is to be derived or interpreted from three pairs of shells doing that which you see evidence for on the ground and from the other witnesses, and as shown in this plan, going from south to north, with the changes of distance that you've spoken of?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I see this as a very professional piece of artillery work. I believe that it was -- the rounds were observed as they were landing and the fire was adjusted, and the fire was adjusted in a way that seems to me to be, "Add 100, add 50," from an observer who would be in a general southerly direction from the target to be engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What might have been the intended object of this shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I think it is most likely that the intended target was the radio station on the banks of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reason for that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Two rounds, 5 and 6, bracketed the area, and then the firing ceased. Normally, artillery fire ceases when the target has been successfully engaged. There was nothing else in that area that I could see that would be a likely target.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say "bracketed the area", two questions that you might deal with, and we'll come back to the type of artillery piece in a minute. But given the artillery piece you believe this to have been, what degree of accuracy can be achieved? And the second question involved with that is how near to a target does a shell have to land in order for the shelling to count as a success?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: A shell of the nature of that size, of about 122 millimetres, would have a lethal radius of something in the region of 40 to 50 metres, and it would have a danger radius of around 300 metres. So if a round fell within 25 or 30 metres of the target, it would neutralise it, and I would say that that is an acceptable level of accuracy for neutralisation purposes. By "neutralise", we mean put out of action, prevent from engaging in the activity which it had been engaged in beforehand. It doesn't necessarily mean destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accuracy of this sort of shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: The D-30 J, firing the type of ammunition which I believe it fired, has a beaten zone at a maximum range of around 45 metres by 10 metres. That means that about 50 per cent of the shells will fall in an elliptical pattern; fired from the same gun, at the same bearing, at the same elevation, will fall within an area 45 metres long by 10 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So on your plan, you've drawn a possible location of an observer, and is the general position that where artillery is being aimed from many kilometres away, you need an observer to see where the first shell lands?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: You need an observer generally to see where every shell lands, unless the target has previously been adjusted and recorded or a similar target within certain very limited parameters has already been engaged by that particular type of weapon within, again, a particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why do you choose this line as the line along which a possible observer might have been positioned?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I think it's quite likely. It could also have been in the opposite direction to the north. But if you look at the three sets of rounds, the first set, the second set, MPI-corrected, and the third set all give an "add or a drop" pattern. Given that the north side or the east side of the river was in ABiH hands completely, and given that there was high ground to the south, you can just see on the edge of the map the beginning of the contour lines leading to high ground where an observer could be stationed. Similarly, there were very high buildings in this area which could have housed an observer who could have been relaying information to guns by radio or by telephone, if telephones were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've also marked the nearest military installation or, rather, an arrow in its direction. Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: This is the nearest military installation. It is 310 metres from the closest round, which was number 3. Yet after number 3 was fired, 5 and 6 were fired in a direction away from that particular military installation. Therefore, I concluded it was not the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was that military installation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I'd have to examine my notes. The headquarters of the 301st Mechanised Brigade of the Armija located in the Prostor building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then if we could mark your summary, which I think you've gone through your summary and checked it for accuracy, have you not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll mark that, with the Court's leave, as an exhibit. But two other issues. In order to identify the type of artillery piece, were you provided with a bag or container of remnants from the shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That contained two fuses?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: It did, and various bits of shell case fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the fuses showed you what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: The fuses showed me, given the writing on them, showed me that it was, in fact, an OF 462 Z shell which was fired. The reason I say that is because the fuses themselves were RGM-2 fuses, which are specifically fitted to that type of shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, was that type of shell in use by any of the warring parties in the former Yugoslavia at the time of this shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That shelling was only used by the D-30 J, which was a Yugoslav-built variant of a Warsaw Pact weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did any of the warring parties have access to that weaponry at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: To my belief, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that weapon have a known and defined range?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: It does. Firing that particular shell, it has a defined maximum range of 15 thousand and about 280 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With the knowledge that you had then collected, did you try and find out where it might have been fired from, these shells?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Using the map that's on the board and the pointer -- there's a loudspeaker that should pick up your voice -- could you explain to the Judges what it was, please, that you -- and for counsel, what it was you were able to conclude?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Based on the fact that the shell came from -- the shells came from the west, due west, from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: The shells came due west into Zenica. Therefore, I went west along the road between Vitez and Travnik and examined the area, and I found a feature in Puticevo which provided ideal gun platforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at the map, we see the front line for the Serb troops to the west of that. Could the gun concerned or the artillery piece concerned have been fired from within Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Under no circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were it to have been fired from the Puticevo feature, would that have been at maximum range, or near maximum range, or what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: It would have been very close to maximum range.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why did you prefer that as a possible site to any of the intervening places at a shorter distance between there and Zenica itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: The weapon would have been firing on maximum charge, which would have meant a noise level of something in the region of 180 decibels; an extremely loud noise, in other words, which would have been heard over a very wide area. If it had been much closer to Zenica, it would have been within distance -- hearing distance of Armija locations. I heard no reports that anyone had heard rounds being fired on that day. Therefore, I concluded, from logic, that it was a good distance away from where Armija units were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just remind the Judges. Roughly, where were the BiH positions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: The Armija were located in Travnik itself, in Zenica, and somewhat west of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if we are to get through this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I've probably concluded. In any case, everything else contained in your summary, including the comments that are made about launch time and so on, may this summary become Exhibit 2816, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll do my best to finish today, but I can't guarantee it. But let's get started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You served as a United Nations military observer in Sarajevo from May of 1993 to August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So you were in the country when the shelling actually occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is not correct. The shelling occurred on the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, April the 19th, 1993. But you undertook no contemporaneous investigation of the shelling incident at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Throughout your tour of duty as a United Nations military observer, you never witnessed any deliberate attacks on civilian targets, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I witnessed attacks on targets in which there were civilians, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On page 2 of your statement, sir, five years ago, you said: "I never witnessed myself a deliberate attack on civilian areas from the sector in which I was working." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: From the sector in which I was working, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: From the sector in which I was working at the time, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you've given two separate statements to the Prosecution's investigators, is that right, one in 1995 and one in 1997?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In the 1995 statement, there wasn't any question asked of you about the Zenica shelling incident, was there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I was not aware of the Zenica shelling incident at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So your first involvement, and I think you've said this, was in 1997, four years after the shelling had actually occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that was the first time that you actually made a visit to the site, four years later; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were asked to take a look at this incident, I take it you studied the file in the Tribunal or in the Prosecution's office in The Hague. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you see -- have you reviewed the testimony of Major Baggesen in this case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the testimony of Colonel Landry in this case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the testimony of Professor Jankovic, a ballistics engineer in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Are you a ballistics engineer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I'm not. I'm an artillery officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Have you reviewed the testimony of the investigating judge who investigated this incident in Zenica, Mladen Veseljak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I may have done. At this stage, I don't remember. If I did, it was at that time in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you actually seen the extensive report that was produced by Mladen Veseljak concerning the Zenica shelling incident, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder if I could ask for the booklet of exhibits that I've put together to be distributed to everybody. For everybody's convenience, they are highlighted. Just for your information, Mr. Hamill, they are separately tabbed. We'll have an exhibit number attached, and then I'll refer to a tab number and you should see what I'm referring to highlighted in your copy, sir. I wonder if I could ask you to turn first in this exhibit, after it's been given a number by the registrar --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be D202/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you turn, sir, to Tab 6. This is a copy of the report that was prepared by the investigating judge, Mladen Veseljak, on the 19th of April, 1993. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I honestly couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If you could just turn to page 2, sir, the investigating judge recites that: "Many large and smaller shell fragments were found at the scene. Based on a fuse found at the scene, members of the crime squad concluded that the shells were fired from a 150-millimetre calibre, and shell fragments were then taken for further expert analysis." Were you aware of that conclusion, 155-millimetre calibre?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to Judge Veseljak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No, but it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you review the testimony of the artillery expert used in the Blaskic case, Mr. Sefjulah Mrkajlevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, it's true, sir, is it not, that the European Community Monitoring Mission prepared absolutely no reports that you've seen concerning this shelling incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Where did you get the shell fragments from, sir? Who gave them to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I was given them in the police station in Zenica by a representative of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware that Mr. Mrkajlevic, in the Blaskic case, testified that all the shell fragments had been turned over to the Canadian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you see any chain of custody records concerning what you just --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You have to wait for the interpreters, to be fair to them. Have you seen any chain of custody records confirming that this bag, or whatever it was that you were given, containing bits and pieces and two fuses had been kept in the custody of the MUP or the Ministry of the Interior from the time of the shelling until the time that they were turned over to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that it's impossible for these shells to have been fired from Serb positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I say it's impossible for them to have been fired from Serb positions if, in fact, the fuses which were given to me were the fuses which detonated those rounds which exploded in Zenica on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We'll get to the fuses in just a second, sir. But could you turn to Tab 10. I'm sorry, Tab 11. This is a report that was prepared by the European Community Monitoring Mission concerning a shelling incident on Vitez and on Zenica May the 9th, 1993, and the actual shelling occurred the day before. Have you ever seen this report before?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And this report concludes that 152-millimetre shells were fired from the Vlasic feature from Bosnian Serb artillery on both locations; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: It says that, but that's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, there is no question, sir, is there, that Bosnian Serb artillery had Zenica in range from its positions in Vlasic, as you can see from that exhibit. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, but the point is, the point is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No need to argue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: The point is that the weapons that were used at the time, on that day on the 19th, bears no relationship to that question. They were 122-millimetre D-30 J's based on the fact that the fuses that I was given were in fact fuses that were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You say that the RGM-2 fuse is used in the OF 62 shell that is fired from a 122-millimetre weapon; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: The fuse is very specific to a particular shell, which is the OF 482Z, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Actually, the RGM-2 fuse is used in a 152-millimetre shell of a designated OF 540; isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: If it is, I wasn't made aware of that until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And equally true, sir, the RGM-2 fuse is used in a 130-millimetre shell designated OF 482, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I base that finding on books which were given to me of the weaponry of the Yugoslav army, in none of which I could find the RGM fuse used for anything other than this particular shell, which was used for this particular gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sir, you presumably have read the testimony of Professor Jankovic in the Blaskic case, where he makes precisely that point, that those fuses, the RGM-2 type fuses, are used in three separate calibers, 120-millimetre, 152-millimetre, and 130-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That may be the case, but I can say from the firing tables that I was given, I could find no other reference to the RGM-2 fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You are not saying, sir, I take it, that a RGM-2 fuse is not used in a 152-millimetre shell, or a 130-millimetre shell, as testified by the ballistic engineer, Professor Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you, please, slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I am not saying that. What I am saying is that given the information that I had, the only reference that I could find to it in Yugoslav field manuals was in relation to a 122-millimetre shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning to the reports that Judge Veseljak prepared. He makes a reference to one fuse found at the scene. If you take a look at page 2 of Tab 6, sir. "Based on a fuse found at the scene, members of the crime squad concluded that the shells fired were of 155-millimetre calibre." Where did the other fuse come from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I have absolutely no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement on page 2, that April the 19th was the first occasion on which the city of Zenica was shelled?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I was given to understand that by people at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that Zenica had actually been shelled the night before, on the 18th of April, 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Sayers. The witness has just said that what he was told was that they were shelled the first time on the 19th. He's obviously not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't like to play games with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you just turn to Tab 4, sir, which is an ECMM document. The local situation in Zenica, which says: "The situation is quiet, as these lines are being typed, throughout the night and the day there was sporadic shelling." And the date is April 18, 1993. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No one told you that. All right. You said that at 800 mils elevation, or 45 degrees, a D-30 J weapon has a 50 per cent probability of landing in what you referred to as a beaten zone, which is an ellipse, 45 metres by 10 metres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Which also means that it has a 50 per cent probability of not landing in that beaten zone, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: It does, but the probability curve can be worked out statistically. It's not very large. Ninety-nine per cent of rounds will fall within an area 90 metres by 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: -- 95 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you would agree that that accuracy of the fall of shot depends upon a wide number of variables, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And we'll go into those in just a minute. You also said that the D-30 J weapon has a slow rate of fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me put it to you, Mr. Hamill: D-30 J can fire eight rounds per minute, can't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: It may well do, but that is at extreme stress on the crews. Generally, I would have said five rounds per minute, max.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One every 12 seconds, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But at eight rounds a minute, that's one every seven-and-a-half seconds?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Seven-and-a-half seconds, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that the -- what information did you have that the HVO actually had 122-millimetre calibre weapons in their arsenal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let's take a look at Tab 1, sir, which is a milinfosum dated November the 15th, 1992, number 16. And I turn you to page 3, where there is a reference to an HVO 203-millimetre gun, nicknamed Nora by local villagers. Were you aware that the HVO had a 203-millimetre weapon nicknamed Nora?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I was not. But I was aware that the Yugoslav army had been well equipped with artillery before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Similarly, sir, if you would just turn to Tab 16. There is a report on page 3, paragraph 11A, of two 155-millimetre Nora howitzers in the Mosunj quarry. It says it remains to be corroborated, but were you aware that the HVO had 155-millimetre weapons in their inventory?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: As I said, I am aware that the -- all the factions had various weapons, because the JNA was extremely well equipped with artillery. And again, if you look at this, this contradicts your last comment where the Nora was described as 203-millimetre -- talked about 155-millimetre Noras.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Now, the ABiH also had heavy artillery, did they not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: For example, if you look at Tab 2, they had 152-millimetre weapons available to them, or larger; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And if you also take a look at Tab 12, sir, the ABiH, at least, if you look at paragraph 8C, had 122-millimetre D30 weapons in their inventory, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I don't doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, indeed, that howitzer at 122 millimetres was observed in the Travnik area firing at Vitez, or in the Vitez direction, on the 13th of May 1993, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: So it appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you always found the Bosnian Serbs to be very secretive about their artillery assets, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it was known that Bosnian Serb artillery had positions high on the Vlasic feature at Mount Palinik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Which is, I think, 1.933 metres above sea level or about 6.000 feet high, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: May well be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And there is no question, sir, that the Bosnian Serb army had in its inventory 155-millimetre weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: This is irrelevant to this particular shelling, because the shelling did not come from Vlasic. It came from the west. Vlasic is to the north-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you'd answer my question, sir. The Bosnian Serb army had 155-millimetre ordnance in their arsenal, did they not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And 152-millimetre ordnance, 130-millimetre ordnance, right, and 122-millimetre ordnance?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you turn to Tab 21, page 2. A gentleman from whom we've heard in this case, a gentleman with the 3rd Corps, I can't remember his name, so I won't mention it. I can't remember whether he was in closed session, so I won't mention the name, but you can read it there. This gentleman from the 3rd Corps stated that various four to six rounds had fallen in the town centre in Zenica, and that these rounds had been fired from Bosnian Serb artillery held positions on the Vlasic feature. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So once again, sir, there is no question, is there, that Zenica was in range of Bosnian Serb artillery on the Vlasic feature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, when were you informed that this shelling started?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I was informed the shelling started at 1210 hours on the 19th of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Would you turn to Tab 5, please. This is an entry from the battlefield diary or war diary prepared by Major Baggesen, Exhibit D75/1. Have you spoken to Major Baggesen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If you turn to the 19th of April, you can see that he records in his contemporaneous diary the fact that the attack began at 0930 hours. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is that the first time that you are aware of that information?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And the shelling continued, according to Major Baggesen's war diary, into the afternoon. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, it's true, as you can see from other entries in Major Baggesen's war diary, that Zenica was shelled fairly regularly after April the 19th, 1993. Let me give you a few examples. If you turn to the entry for April the 21st, where 130 people were wounded in a shelling incident. Were you aware that a shelling had occurred just two days later?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know who fired those shells?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And just anyone can read it. I'll just read out the dates: April the 22nd, April the 26th, fired at 1130 at night. Incidentally, Mr. Hamill, it would be rather difficult for a forward observer to walk shots in at 1130 at night; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: By the way, you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, can you please stick to the testimony in chief, because this is expertise. We are not going to go through to the whole shelling from the beginning of Zenica. Can we stick to the expert itself. Because we can ask this witness: Do you know this and this? And he doesn't know. This is not the sense of the -- of his testimony anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I think that the -- it is material, however, that Zenica was regularly shelled, and this individual who has been -- or this gentleman, who is being produced as an expert, didn't even know about that, and I wasn't told about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think that's going to help. Look, he just deals with one particular shelling, and he gives evidence about it. And we would be helped, really, if you are contradicting his evidence, if you deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you -- I mean, I don't want to interfere with your cross-examination, but it may help if we know the direction you are heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The direction -- the direction is that there is simply no way for anybody to tell where the shells came from, or what the calibre was on April the 19th, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, ask him some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to crater analysis, sir, you say in your statement, statement number one, five years ago, that crater analysis can give you just a general sense of direction from which incoming fire was actually fired. But it's not possible to determine the range from forensic examination of a shell crater; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, to do a crater analysis, the first thing you need is a very accurate compass, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Because you need to know what the magnetic deviation of the particular compass is, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's certainly relevant, when you are doing this compass analysis, or compass reading, to try to determine the direction from which the shell came, whether there is any magnetic metal in the vicinity, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you just take a look at one of these photographs that you were shown. I don't have a number on mine. It's one of the copies of Exhibit Z2281. Well, actually, why don't you just show him this. If you put that on the ELMO, it might be the best way of doing it. And you can see that there's a large amount of metal around that particular crater, can't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: There is a certain amount of metal, but if you move far enough away from it, your compass won't get disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the people that measured the angle of incoming fire with their compass moved far enough away from those metallic features when they did their analysis on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I don't know what they did, but I know what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, do you know what the magnetic deviation of the compass used by Major Baggesen and his colleague, Mr. Lausten, was on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No. But I do know what the magnetic deviation of my compass was. I used a tested prismatic compass.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And a tested prismatic compass is preferable to use, because it actually lists the magnetic deviation on it, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How do you determine what the magnetic deviation of your compass was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: My compass was tested to be accurate, so it was accurate. And all I had to do was place the magnetic deviation of Zenica on it, which I got from a local map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you first visited Zenica in 1997 to look at the scene, it's true that insufficient traces remained to conduct any kind of an accurate crater analysis; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: There are degrees of accuracy involved. I saw nothing in my analysis which differed from the analysis which I had been given as Major Baggesen's analysis. And even allowing for some deviation, we are talking about gross error here. The shells, obviously came, even to an untutored eye, from the west, generally west.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at some of the variables that -- that are -- that affect the accuracy of fall of shot, sir. The first variable, or set of variables, the purely mechanical variables, the actual ordnance itself. One would be the so-called tube life, the amount -- the number of rounds that have actually been shot through the gun tube. The more rounds that have been shot through the tube, the less accurate the piece becomes. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't know what the tube life of a particular piece of ordnance at issue was, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The next variable is the quality of the explosive propellant actually used. Because with uneven burning characteristics, the trajectory of the expelled shell can be affected. Wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you don't know what kind of propellant was used on the shell at issue, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The next set of variables are the meteorological variables, if you like. Any proficient artillery officer, before he fires off a round at a specific target, has to know, for example, the air temperature, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That's very useful, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Because the hotter the air, the less dense it is, and therefore the greater the range. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: In general terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the denser the air, the less the range, or the steeper the fall of shot?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the air temperature was on the 19th of April, when you say the shelling occurred around midday?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The next variable is barometric pressure. You have to know that, because that affects air density and, in fact, air density influences the fall of shot as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And do you know what the barometric pressure was around midday on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I am given to understand it was roughly standard temperature and pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: People on the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can you identify anybody particularly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Specifically, at this stage, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, I can certainly understand that contemporary observers would be able to tell you what the temperature may have been on that day, but how would they have been able to tell you the barometric pressure on that day, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Some people are sensitive to pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The next variable, sir, is winds aloft. You need to know the strength and direction of the wind through the various levels that the shell passes during its ballistic trajectory, because winds aloft effect the direction of flight. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it's typical, isn't it, that the higher you go, the harder the winds blow, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Generally speaking, that would be acceptable, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, what is the top of the ballistic trajectory above sea level of a D30 J 122-millimetre, do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: As I don't have the ballistic tables at hand, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me suggest to you that the maximum height that a 122-millimetre shell can reach at a 45-degree angle, which is a maximum firing angle would be 6.000 metres, or approximately 19.000 to 20.000 feet. Do you know what the winds aloft were on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be fair to say, sir, that you have no information that the HVO had any kind of meteorological facilities whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Another factor that you have to take into account is the Coriolis force, the rotation of the earth. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That's correct at extreme ranges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And this was fired, in your opinion, at extreme range?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Very likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, other variables include the actual range -- I mean, the more extreme the range, the less accurate the weapon becomes. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And conversely, the closer you are, the more accurate the fall of shot would be expected to be?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: It doesn't actually work like that. It depends on whether you've got one fixed charge or a number of charges. Generally, if you have a weapon with, say, five charges, then at the maximum extent of each charge the inaccuracy will be greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know how many charges were used on the 19th of April 1993, in any of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: All I can say is that if it was fired at 15.000 metres, or thereabouts, it was fired at maximum charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know -- well, another variable is the accuracy of the maps available to the artillery commander. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Strictly speaking, yes. And that's why we fire adjusting rounds, which was done on this occasion to shoot out barometric temperature, Coriolis, and other variations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Similarly, another variable is the accuracy of the firing data charts that are actually maintained in the command post. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And do you know anything about those, whether they were accurate or not for this particular weapon on the date at issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you seriously asking the witness if he knew what was in the command post on the 19th of April? Mr. Sayers --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's a more generic question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the HVO had accurate firing charts available, generally speaking, sir, for this particular type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: From whom did you discover that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I spent a long time in the area and in the mission, and I know a lot of people. I have spoken to HV, I have spoken to HVO, I have spoken to Armija, I have spoken to VRS people, and it's quite obvious that if they have the weapons, they have the firing tables to go with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. One final variable is the level of training of the particular gun layers in the artillery battery members. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the HVO artillery members were well trained or anything about their training?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: It's clear from their shooting that they were well trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's clear from whoever shot the weapon that they were well trained; wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I would say it's clear from the HVO shooting, generally, that they are well trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, one sure way to determine the source and range of artillery fire is artillery locating radar. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If you just turn to Tab 9, sir. I think it's Tab 9. You can see that the ECMM addresses arguments regarding another shelling incident in Zenica, or Vitez I believe, April the 27th, 1993, arguing about the source of the shelling: "And the ECMM monitor strongly felt that the situation could be resolved, once and for all, if locating battery could be made available to clarify the situation." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the next tab on page 2 makes the contention that the problem of verifying firing units and targets must be solved so that there is no question as who is firing on who. The only way to do that is by artillery-locating radar. Do you concur with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Within limits, I concur with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. That would certainly have eliminated any doubt at all, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I would have done it, had it been available.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Now, did you expect any of the shell fragments collected by Mr. Lausten which were turned over to the Canadian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the shell fragments that you inspected, sir, in 1997, fours year after the incident, were the shell fragments that were collected by either Mr. Lausten or Judge Veseljak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: As I already made clear, I went on information that was given to me at the time, and I cannot speak for the chain of evidence, and I cannot say exactly where the fuses came from, nor the fragments, merely what they meant to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And to be perfectly fair to you, Mr. Hamill, you did say on page 4 of your 1997 statement that you looked at two RGM-2 fuses, and that these fuses purported to come from shells fired on Zenica on April the 19th. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you are not sure of that fact, are you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that you do not yourself know, and you have not performed any calculations yourself of the angle of descent of the shells that landed in Zenica on April the 19th?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's not possible --

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: It is not possible to do that type of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Have you ever seen any treatises or technical data on how to do crater analysis, anything that's in writing, any published treatises or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you identify one for us, so we can all see how to go about doing it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Sorry, I am not with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can you identify for the Court, and for us, any authoritative treatise on how to do a proper crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a name, but I have used two; one produced by artillery school, and one produced by, if I remember right, the Royal Artillery in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have given us your conclusions regarding the source of the artillery fire. You say that -- I believe that it was at the eastern end of the Puticevo feature; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Based on the information that I was given, I would estimate that that was the most likely place to locate artillery of that type to fire into Zenica on that bearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether the HVO actually had any artillery assets there that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And no one has contended to you that any such artillery assets were located there that day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Come on. Look, he is an expert. He comes here to give his evidence of the analysis which he made. He is not giving hearsay evidence or anything of the sort. The witness has told us how he has come to his conclusions. You may challenge those conclusions, Mr. Sayers, but there is no point asking a series of hypotheses and a series of matters which he might or might not be aware of. Now, let us concentrate on his analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me address one other question, sir. You eliminated, as a possibility, the site of the quarry at Mali Mosunj as being the potential firing point, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I think that the reason that you did that would be that that would have required an angle to the -- from the quarry to the point of the centre of Zenica, where the shells fell, at 4.500 mils, or about 253 degrees true, right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you concluded that a 17-degree difference would be just too much, given the ECMM conclusions of their investigation on the 19th of April, and yours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And so, sir, you would discount the Mali Mosunj quarry as being the firing point, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: In my opinion, I discount it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, on page 5 of your statement three years ago, you said that it's possible that the shells were fired closer to Zenica than either the Puticevo feature or the Mosunj quarry, given the confused nature of the front at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you still abide by that opinion today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. If you could just turn to the last tab on this document, sir, there are a series of statistics from the U.S. Department of Defence, December of 1995, entitled, "Bosnia Country Handbook." Looking at the D-30 J weapon, the extended range on that weapon is listed at 17.300 metres. Were you aware of that before today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So the conventional range is 15.300 metres, but the extended range is actually 2.000 metres more than that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Using a different projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What kind of projectile?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, it was an M-95, but I wouldn't swear to it. Correction, it was not an M-95, it was an -- it was not the OF 482.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I read about it at the time in the firing manuals issued by the Yugoslav national army or the Yugoslav People's Army, and the fuse that they used was a different fuse to the RGM-2 on that particular shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If you take a look at the last page here, there's data on 152-millimetre howitzer M-84. The conventional range on that weapon is 17.200, and the extended range is 24.400 metres; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That weapon, as I said before, sir, uses an OF 540 shell, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you do not know that that OF 540 shell is detonated by an RGM-2 fuse?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the page before that is a 130-millimetre weapon, an M-46. The conventional range of that weapon is 27.490 metres. Let me just ask you, sir, were you able to determine, from the fragments that were given to you, that the shell fired was actually a 122-millimetre calibre?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you handed a large fragment of the shell that was quite intact, or were these very small pieces that were in the bag that was given to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: They were very small pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And were you aware that Judge Veseljak actually collected a very large fragment that he found to be quite intact?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, with all due respect, I think, you should stop this kind of exercise. This is not the first time that you go back to what Judge Veseljak did, and the witness has already told you that he was not abreast of the investigation conducted by this judge, that he did not follow all that, and you are turning around an expert opinion. Are you contesting it or not? If you do, then challenge and tell us what you are challenging, or if you are not an expert, you may also, at a given moment, call in an expert who will challenge this expert opinion. We have testimony here which is very strictly confined to an area, which is an expert opinion on the shelling of Zenica at a particular moment in time and with some conclusions which this witness is offering us, and I believe you should adhere to this. We cannot continue like this, going into things, establishing what the witness knows, what he doesn't. Tell us, what you are challenging in this testimony itself? You are going around this expert opinion. You are not addressing this opinion directly. Either tell us what you want, really, what you are challenging in this case, or then call a witness of your own.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but the only point to the question was that I was trying to establish that this gentleman was not given all of the shell fragments that were actually collected by the gentleman that did the investigation on the 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've covered the shell fragments. We've got the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just put it to you, Mr. Hamill, that if a 152-millimetre shell uses an RGM-2 fuse, and if a 130-millimetre shell uses an RGM-2 fuse, as does a 122-millimetre shell, OF 462, and you're given just the fuses and some small fragments, you can't tell what the calibre of the shell was that actually hit Zenica on the 19th of April, 1993, in all fairness, can you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: If it is the case that other weapons use that fuse, contrary to the information that I was given at the time, then of course I accept that. As I said earlier on consistently, my report is written purely on the facts as I knew them and information that I was able to ferret out from forces in the Armija, for example, who provided me with the range tables for the full range of Yugoslav weapons of the day. And nowhere did I find a reference to that particular fuse, except for the D-30 J. Now, if you're telling me it is used somewhere, then I have to say that in the range tables, which are the official range tables of those weapons, I saw no reference to it, because believe me, I looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand, sir, and I don't mean to challenge you, but I just mean to put to you the position very simply. If those weapons, all three of them, use -- of different calibres use RGM-2 fuses, then you can't tell what calibre of weapon actually hit Zenica or what calibre of shell hit Zenica on the 19th of April, can you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: [Inaudible] that a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, sir, no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few things, if I may, in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the time of your own personal inspection, the craters had lost definition, to a degree, I think.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Some of the craters had lost definition to a greater degree than others, but some of them were still very, very clear. The one at the bus stop was quite clear, and what I described as number 1, the first shell to land, based on the testimony of other people, was also still very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So from your own inspection at that time, how many compass degrees of error or allowance have to be made, in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I would say that it came in on a true bearing of 4.800 mils in the case of number 1. Number 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you again. I'll come to that in a second. But by the time of the loss of definition of the craters, insofar as there had been a loss, do we have to allow for any greater error or margin of error at the time of your inspection than, for example, at the time of the inspection by the ECMM monitors?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: It depends on the type of blurring. In the case of one shell, in particular, there was no blurring, as such, and the marks were very, very clear and related very, very closely to the photographs that I had seen that were taken on the day or, correction, that purportedly were taken on the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So overall, taking into account the photographs, the ECMM monitors' assessments and your own inspection of these craters, within how many degrees do you say it was due west?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I am satisfied that it came in due west.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we look at your plan, because you've been asked about the Mosunj quarry and we can see it marked on the plan, is that, in any sense, a candidate site or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: In my view, it is not a candidate site. But further, it was also HVO held at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Vlasic feature, which you've been asked about but we haven't yet just identified it on the map, can you tell us where it is by compass bearing or by pointing it out?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: The Vlasic mountain extends north of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any possibility of that being the source of these artillery shells?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: The Vlasic Mountain extends north of Travnik, and that is generally in a north-westerly direction. This is clearly 45 degrees or 800 mils from 4.800 mils. Now, if I excluded rounds coming in from 4.500 mils, I'm certainly excluded rounds coming in from roughly 5.200 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple more questions. The fragments, you weren't able to say from what size of shell they came. Were they consistent or inconsistent with the possibility of their coming from the shell you've described?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: They were just shell fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. These fuse manuals and so on that you looked at coming from the JNA, in your experience, are these documents exhaustive and complete?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: They are extremely exhaustive and they are extremely complete, and they relate to every aspect of what your learned colleague mentioned earlier on, such as wind speed and direction, barometric pressure, chart temperature, air temperature, and it gives the variations for each of those at an exhaustive list of ranges, generally in terms of pair hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the manuals that told you of the use to which fuses were put for particular shells, again in your experience, how exhaustive are they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: These were the same manuals. What I examined was the manuals of the particular weapons, which gave the shell types, their fuses, the ranges and the elevations that one would use.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And no sign of this fuse to you being used for any other weapon -- for any other shell available to the JNA at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I looked through them exhaustively in order to find what shells would have used that fuse, and I must say I didn't find it. That is not to say that such shells do not exist. But I, in my exhaustive examination of the JNA manuals, could find no reference to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But when you were being -- I must be careful I'm not going too fast. When you were being asked about variables, one of them was the absence of meteorological information. But here you're postulating the use of an observer, and you use the term "adjusting rounds", which may need defining. With an observer, does the absence of meteorological information necessarily become significant?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: With an observer, the absence of meteorological information or accurate mapped data is unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what are "adjusting rounds"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Generally, the information is given to the gun position by the observer as to the location of the target, and the battery, or single gun, or a combination of guns in question fires what is called an adjusting round. The observer sees where this round falls in relation to the target, and he gives a correction down to the guns by way of left or right, add or drop, in relation to his position to the target. Then a second round or group of rounds is fired, and again the observer checks to see where they are in relation to the target, and generally the third set of rounds would be accurate, they would be on target. We have seen an example of it, according to the testimony given to me during my investigation, in this particular shelling, which was a classic example, to my mind, of, "Add 100, add 50," or alternatively, "Drop 100, drop 50," if the observer were in the north, that is, on the other side of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if the third rounds hadn't been on target, what would you then have seen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: It would have called for an additional set of rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, on the question of the timing or the time of the shelling, you've told us about your information and the times given to you, and you've told us about how the order of the shelling was always consistent in its account or consistent in its account. Were you having people describing hearing one shell and then getting out of the way and finding another one; is that the way the story gets told?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: More or less. It depended on the individual in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: But as I say, the consistency was that there was a very short period of time between each of the two in the groups, in the three groups. One witness said, "Maybe two seconds." Another one said, "Oh, maybe four or five seconds." But it was a short period of time, certainly less than seven and a half seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then the time between the rounds, as you got them, were, I think, 12.10 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The final two at 12.29?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked about whether you've read Professor Jankovic's report, and you have, or his testimony. Is there anything you want to add by way of dealing with it now or have you dealt with it in the course of answering Mr. Sayers' questions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I think I dealt with it in the course of answering your learned colleague's questions, but I would say that generally it was irrelevant to this particular case, and how relevant it is to the remainder of the trial, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Irrelevant because?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: Because it didn't deal with this particular type of shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been challenged as to whether you've been, as it were, available to inspect this at the time, I think. At the time, were you dealing with another shelling or did you deal with another shelling in the course of your time in Bosnia, the market shelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I did, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I do not believe that was challenged, Your Honour, and that was not raised on direct or cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I believe you did deal with the Merkale shelling in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN GERARD BRENTON HAMILL
utterances.text: I did, but that was 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Nothing else, thank you. And I'm grateful to the Chamber for sitting to accommodate the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Hamill, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position tomorrow is that there are the two witnesses who probably will be quite short. There's the third witness we have been speaking of and I won't name who we've been hoping to get here and eventually discovered we were going to be able to get, as I understand it. So there will be three witnesses tomorrow. There are a number of administrative matters and one or two rulings still to be dealt with. You have, I hope, now received not only the Defence skeleton argument in relation to formal statements and affidavits, but I hope you've received a document from us, including a schedule, by way of response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been filed, and I'm sorry it hasn't found its way through. I'm sure it will come through in one form or another tonight. There have been some issues about transcripts and one or two other issues, but it may be possible, because I know that this would be the desire of the Chamber, to conclude matters tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are the video arguments in comprehensible form?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. There is another schedule being produced over the weekend, much more complete, I think, and I hope it addresses the Defence concerns. Indeed, I think now it is much fuller in relation to the identification of transcripts to videos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And is it on its way?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because if we're going to deal with these matters, we must have these schedules tonight. I don't know if the Registry can help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if we're allowed to approach you in the informal way, other than through the Registry, then I can, as soon as I leave here, ensure that the documents are made available to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you do that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to the Defence as well, if there are any of them that they are missing at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the Defence should have them too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may address the Court very, very briefly. As our colleague Mr. Nice just said, we have been also informed about the possibility of having a witness -- I guess I cannot use his name. That was a witness under number 10 in previous listings of transcripts. We have been told about that possibility of his appearance an hour ago, indeed while we had the afternoon break, for the first time, and that is not in accordance with the batting order by which we should have been informed in at least 14 days, and then within that frame it might have been changed, whether first day or last day, but it was not listed. Indeed, this witness was listed last time -- forgive me if I'm wrong, but many months ago; sometime, I guess, in October or November. And after that, the case was dropped. He appeared in the list of possible transcripts, and we were not informed about the possibility he's coming here. We simply, under this -- after so many trial hours in the courtroom continuously, I don't see the possibility that we can really prepare this witness for tomorrow morning. He had been testifying in two other cases; in one of them, quite a great deal of testifying. There are a couple of his earlier statements, and I really see the problem here. I'm not raising that objection just as a formality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, I'm sure. But there has been talk of this witness being called. His transcript was produced, and he's been on the list for a great deal of time. Well, Mr. Kovacic, see how you get on tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In French they say, and I believe that in other languages the same holds true, that you should sleep on it and you'll be wiser in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not too much sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. Since we did study at that time many transcripts, and luckily this one fell in the category to be discussed, I have to admit that I did not read it, really. I mean I went through, and that was three weeks ago, if I'm not wrong. So if I'm preparing a witness, if he was testifying in two cases, I have to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, see what you can do, as I say, by way of preparation. If need be, we shall have to sit on Friday morning to accommodate you, but I hope that can be avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, sir. I certainly will. And in some earlier occasions, if I'm not wrong, you did admit that such a witness could appear later for cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In this case not, because this is right at the end of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And not to add that he is a very repetitive witness as well. He's maybe not needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's also the Witness AO issue that needs to be resolved, the sooner the better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We shall have that in mind for tomorrow. Very well. Nine tomorrow, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
